The most capable of foreseeing the dangers were the very ones who expected to benefit from them; and even the most prudent judged it not inexpedient to sacrifice one part of their freedom to secure the rest, just as a wounded man has his arm cut off to save the rest of his body.
danishChanges.after: Der skulle langt mindre til end denne tale for at rive uvidende og letforførte mennesker med. De havde desuden for mange stridigheder til at kunne undvære voldgiftsmænd og for megen grådighed og ærgerrighed til længe at kunne undvære herrer. Alle løb deres lænker i møde i den tro, at de sikrede deres frihed. De havde fornuft nok til at se fordelene ved en politisk orden, men ikke erfaring nok til at forudse farerne. Netop dem, der bedst kunne forudse misbrugene, regnede med at drage fordel af dem. Selv de kloge mente, at man måtte ofre en del af friheden for at bevare resten, ligesom en såret lader armen skære af for at redde resten af kroppen.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation; restore mur=wall, alignements=boundaries, mal conduit sword qualification; note18.

danishChanges.before: Such was, or may well have been, the origin of society and laws, which laid new fetters on the poor and gave new powers to the rich; which irretrievably destroyed natural liberty, eternally fixed the law of property and inequality, converted clever usurpation into an unalterable right, and, for the advantage of a few ambitious individuals, subjected all mankind to perpetual labor, slavery, and wretchedness. It is easy to see how the establishment of one community made the establishment of all the others necessary, and how, in order to make head against united forces, the rest of mankind had to unite in turn. Societies soon multiplied and spread across the face of the earth until hardly a corner of the world was left in which a man could escape the yoke, and withdraw his head from beneath the sword which he saw perpetually hanging over him by a thread. Civil right having thus become the common rule among the members of each community, the law of nature retained its place only between different communities, where, under the name of the right of nations, it was qualified by certain tacit conventions in order to make commerce practicable and to serve as a substitute for natural compassion—which lost, when applied to societies, almost all the influence it had had over individuals, and survived no longer except in some great cosmopolitan spirits who, breaking down the imaginary barriers that separate different peoples, follow the example of our Sovereign Creator, and include the whole human race in their benevolence.
danishChanges.after: Sådan var, eller må oprindelsen have været til, samfundet og lovene, som lagde nye bånd på de svage og gav de rige nye kræfter. [Note 18] De ødelagde uigenkaldeligt den naturlige frihed, fastslog ejendommens og ulighedens lov for altid, gjorde en snedig tilegnelse til en uigenkaldelig ret og underkastede fra da af hele menneskeslægten arbejde, slaveri og elendighed til fordel for nogle få ærgerrige. Det er let at se, hvordan oprettelsen af ét samfund gjorde alle de andre nødvendige: For at modstå forenede kræfter måtte man selv forene sig. Samfundene voksede hurtigt i antal og omfang og dækkede snart hele jordens overflade. Der var ikke længere et eneste sted, hvor man kunne undslippe åget og få hovedet væk fra det sværd, som altid hang over det og ofte blev ført dårligt. Da den borgerlige ret således var blevet borgernes fælles regel, gjaldt naturloven kun mellem de forskellige samfund. Under navnet folkeret blev den mildnet af visse stiltiende aftaler, som skulle gøre samkvem muligt og erstatte den naturlige medfølelse. Mellem samfund mistede denne nemlig næsten al den kraft, den havde haft mellem mennesker. Den lever kun videre i enkelte store verdensborgersjæle, som overskrider de indbildte grænser mellem folkene og efter deres suveræne skabers eksempel omfatter hele menneskeslægten med deres velvilje.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation; restore mur=wall, alignements=boundaries, mal conduit sword qualification; note18.

danishChanges.before: But political bodies, remaining thus in a state of nature among themselves, soon experienced the inconveniences that had compelled individuals to leave it. Indeed, this state became even more fatal to these great bodies than it had been to the individuals of whom they were composed. From this arose national wars, battles, murders, and reprisals—which shock nature and outrage reason—together with all those horrible prejudices that classify, among the virtues, the honor of shedding human blood. The most distinguished men learned from this to regard cutting one another's throats as a duty; eventually men massacred their fellow creatures by the thousands without so much as knowing why, and committed more murders in a single day's fighting, and more violent outrages in the sack of a single town, than were committed in the state of nature during whole ages over the whole earth. Such were the first effects we can see to have followed the division of mankind into different communities. But let us return to their institutions.
danishChanges.after: De politiske samfund forblev således indbyrdes i naturtilstanden og mærkede snart de ulemper, som havde tvunget de enkelte mennesker til at forlade den. Tilstanden blev endda mere skæbnesvanger mellem disse store legemer, end den havde været mellem de individer, de bestod af. Heraf opstod krige mellem folkene, slag, mord og gengældelser, som får naturen til at gyse og krænker fornuften, sammen med alle de frygtelige fordomme, der regner æren ved at udgyde menneskeblod blandt dyderne. De hæderligste mennesker lærte at regne det for en pligt at skære halsen over på deres medmennesker. Til sidst så man mennesker massakrere hinanden i tusindvis uden at vide hvorfor. På én dags kamp blev der begået flere mord, og ved erobringen af én by flere rædsler, end der i naturtilstanden var blevet begået gennem hele århundreder på hele jorden. Sådan er de første virkninger, vi kan skimte af menneskeslægtens opdeling i forskellige samfund. Lad os vende tilbage til deres oprettelse.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation; restore mur=wall, alignements=boundaries, mal conduit sword qualification; note18.

danishChanges.before: I know that some writers have given other explanations of the origin of political societies, such as the conquest of the powerful, or the association of the weak. It is, indeed, indifferent to my argument which of these causes we choose. The one I have just laid down, however, appears to me the most natural for the following reasons. First: because, in the first case, the right of conquest, being no right in itself, could not serve as the foundation on which to build any other; the victor and the vanquished people still remained, with respect to each other, in the state of war, unless the vanquished, restored to the full possession of their liberty, voluntarily made the victor their chief. For until then, whatever capitulation may have been made, being founded on violence and therefore null and void in itself, there could not on this hypothesis have been either a real society or a body politic, or any law other than that of the strongest. Secondly: because the words strong and weak are, in the second case, ambiguous; for in the interval between the establishment of a right of property, or prior occupancy, and that of political government, the meaning of these words is better expressed by the terms rich and poor, since, in fact, before the institution of laws, men had no other way of reducing their equals to submission than by attacking their goods, or making over some of their own to them. Thirdly: because, as the poor had nothing but their freedom to lose, it would have been in the highest degree absurd for them to resign voluntarily the only good they still enjoyed without getting anything in exchange; whereas the rich, having feelings, if I may put it so, in every part of their possessions, were much easier to harm, and so it was more necessary for them to take precautions against it. And, in short, because it is more reasonable to suppose that a thing was invented by those to whom it would be of service, than by those whom it must have harmed.
danishChanges.after: Jeg ved, at flere har givet andre forklaringer på de politiske samfunds oprindelse, for eksempel den stærkestes erobringer eller de svages sammenslutning. Valget mellem disse årsager er uden betydning for det, jeg vil vise. Alligevel forekommer min forklaring mig mest naturlig af følgende grunde. For det første er erobringsretten ingen ret og kan derfor ikke danne grundlag for andre rettigheder. Erobreren og de erobrede folk bliver ved med at stå i et krigsforhold til hinanden, medmindre folket får sin fulde frihed tilbage og frivilligt vælger sejrherren som leder. Indtil da er enhver overgivelsesaftale grundlagt på vold og derfor i sig selv ugyldig. På dette grundlag kan der hverken findes et virkeligt samfund, et politisk fællesskab eller nogen anden lov end den stærkestes. For det andet er ordene stærk og svag tvetydige i den anden forklaring. Mellem indførelsen af ejendomsretten eller den første besidders ret og oprettelsen af politiske regeringer gengives deres betydning bedre med ordene rig og fattig. Før lovene fandtes, havde et menneske nemlig ingen anden måde at underkaste sig sine ligemænd på end at angribe deres ejendom eller give dem del i sin egen. For det tredje havde de fattige intet andet end deres frihed at miste. Det ville være ren tåbelighed frivilligt at opgive det eneste gode, de havde tilbage, uden at få noget til gengæld. De rige var derimod så at sige følsomme i hver del af deres ejendom og derfor langt lettere at skade. De måtte derfor træffe flere forholdsregler for at beskytte sig. Endelig er det rimeligere at tro, at noget er opfundet af dem, det gavner, end af dem, det skader.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation; restore mur=wall, alignements=boundaries, mal conduit sword qualification; note18.

danishChanges.before: Government had, in its infancy, no regular and constant form. The want of experience and philosophy prevented men from seeing any but present inconveniences, and they only thought of providing against others as they presented themselves. In spite of the efforts of the wisest legislators, the political state remained imperfect, because it was little more than the work of chance; and as it had begun ill, though time revealed its defects and suggested remedies, the original faults were never repaired. It was continually being patched up, when the first task should have been to clear the site and remove all the old materials, as Lycurgus did at Sparta, if a stable and lasting edifice was to be erected. Society consisted at first merely of a few general conventions, which every member bound himself to observe; and for the performance of these covenants the whole body went security to each individual. Experience alone could show the weakness of such a constitution, and how easily it could be infringed with impunity, given the difficulty of convicting men of faults where the public alone was to be witness and judge. The laws could not but be evaded in many ways; disorders and inconveniences could not but multiply continually, until it became necessary to commit the dangerous trust of public authority to private persons, and to entrust the care of enforcing obedience to the deliberations of the people to a magistrate. For to say that chiefs were chosen before the confederacy was formed, and that the administrators of the laws were there before the laws themselves, is too absurd a supposition to consider seriously.
danishChanges.after: Den nye regering havde ingen fast og regelmæssig form. Manglen på erfaring og filosofisk indsigt gjorde, at man kun så de aktuelle ulemper og først tænkte på at afhjælpe andre, når de viste sig. Trods de klogeste lovgiveres indsats forblev den politiske tilstand ufuldkommen, fordi den næsten var tilfældets værk. Den var begyndt forkert, og selv om tiden afslørede mangler og foreslog løsninger, kunne den aldrig rette op på forfatningens grundlæggende fejl. Man lappede hele tiden på den, hvor man burde have begyndt med at rydde grunden og fjerne alle de gamle materialer, som Lykurg gjorde i Sparta, for derefter at opføre en god bygning. Samfundet bestod først kun af nogle få almindelige aftaler, som hver enkelt forpligtede sig til at overholde, og som fællesskabet stod inde for over for den enkelte. Erfaringen måtte vise, hvor svag en sådan ordning var, og hvor let overtræderne kunne undgå at blive afsløret eller straffet, når kun offentligheden skulle være vidne og dommer. Loven måtte omgås på tusind måder, og ulemper og uorden måtte stadig vokse, før man endelig fandt på at betro bestemte personer den farlige opgave at udøve offentlig myndighed og sætte embedsmænd til at håndhæve folkets beslutninger. For påstanden om, at lederne blev valgt, før sammenslutningen fandtes, og at lovenes forvaltere eksisterede før lovene selv, er for urimelig til at blive taget alvorligt.
reasons: Translate English-only DA slot fully against French; distinguish écrit (published work) from English edict misidentification.

danishChanges.before: It would be just as unreasonable to suppose that men at first threw themselves irretrievably and unconditionally into the arms of an absolute master, and that the first expedient which proud and unsubdued men hit upon for their common security was to run headlong into slavery. For what reason, in fact, did they take to themselves superiors, if not in order to be defended from oppression and to have protection for their lives, liberties, and properties, which are, so to speak, the constituent elements of their being? Now in the relations between man and man, the worst that can happen is for one to find himself at the mercy of another; and it would have been inconsistent with common sense to begin by bestowing on a chief the very things they wanted his help to preserve. What equivalent could he offer them for so great a right? And if he had presumed to demand it under the pretext of defending them, would he not have received the answer recorded in the fable: "What more can the enemy do to us?" It is therefore beyond dispute, and indeed the fundamental maxim of all political right, that peoples have set up chiefs to protect their liberty, not to enslave them. "If we have a prince," said Pliny to Trajan, "it is to save us from having a master."
danishChanges.after: Det ville være lige så urimeligt at tro, at folkene fra begyndelsen ubetinget og uigenkaldeligt kastede sig i armene på en enevældig herre, og at stolte, ubøjede menneskers første idé til at sikre sig i fællesskab var at styrte sig ud i slaveri. Hvorfor gav de sig overordnede, hvis ikke for at blive forsvaret mod undertrykkelse og få beskyttet deres ejendom, frihed og liv, som så at sige udgør deres væsens grundbestanddele? Det værste, der kan ske i forholdet mellem to mennesker, er, at det ene bliver prisgivet det andet. Ville det da ikke stride mod al sund fornuft først at overdrage en leder netop de ting, man behøvede hans hjælp til at bevare? Hvad kunne han tilbyde som erstatning for at få en så væsentlig ret? Og hvis han havde vovet at kræve den under påskud af at forsvare dem, ville han så ikke straks have fået fablens svar: »Hvad mere kan fjenden gøre os?« Det er derfor ubestrideligt og den grundlæggende regel i al politisk ret, at folkene har givet sig ledere for at forsvare deres frihed, ikke for at gøre sig til slaver. »Hvis vi har en fyrste,« sagde Plinius til Trajan, »er det for at undgå at få en herre.«
reasons: Translate English-only DA slot fully against French; distinguish écrit (published work) from English edict misidentification.

danishChanges.before: Politicians indulge in the same sophistry about the love of liberty as philosophers do about the state of nature. They judge, by what they see, of very different things they have not seen, and attribute to man a natural propensity to servitude because the slaves within their observation are seen to bear the yoke with patience. They fail to reflect that with liberty it is as it is with innocence and virtue: their value is known only to those who possess them, and the taste for them is lost when they themselves are lost. "I know the charms of your country," said Brasidas to a Persian satrap who was comparing the life at Sparta with that at Persepolis, "but you cannot know the pleasures of mine."
danishChanges.after: De politiske tænkere bruger de samme fejlslutninger om kærligheden til frihed, som filosofferne har brugt om naturtilstanden. Ud fra det, de ser, dømmer de om helt andre ting, som de ikke har set. Fordi de mennesker, de har for øje, tålmodigt bærer slaveriets åg, tillægger de mennesket en naturlig tilbøjelighed til underkastelse. De glemmer, at det med friheden er som med uskylden og dyden: Man kender kun deres værdi, så længe man selv har dem, og mister smagen for dem, så snart man har mistet dem. »Jeg kender dit lands herligheder,« sagde Brasidas til en persisk satrap, der sammenlignede livet i Sparta med livet i Persepolis, »men du kan ikke kende glæderne i mit.«
reasons: Translate English-only DA slot fully against French; distinguish écrit (published work) from English edict misidentification.

danishChanges.before: An unbroken horse erects his mane, paws the ground, and starts back impetuously at the sight of the bridle, while one which is properly trained patiently suffers even whip and spur. So savage man will not bend his neck to the yoke to which civilized man submits without a murmur, but prefers the most turbulent state of liberty to the most peaceful slavery. We cannot, therefore, from the servility of nations already enslaved, judge of the natural disposition of mankind for or against slavery; we should go by the prodigious efforts of every free people to save itself from oppression. I know that the former are forever holding forth in praise of the tranquility they enjoy in their chains, and that they call a state of wretched servitude a state of peace—"the most wretched slavery they call peace" (Tacitus, Histories iv, 17). But when I see the latter sacrificing pleasure, peace, wealth, power, and life itself to the preservation of that one treasure so disdained by those who have lost it; when I see free-born animals dash their brains out against the bars of their cage, from an innate impatience with captivity; when I behold numbers of naked savages who despise European pleasures, braving hunger, fire, the sword, and death to preserve nothing but their independence—I feel that it is not for slaves to argue about liberty.
danishChanges.after: En utæmmet hest rejser manken, stamper i jorden og kæmper voldsomt imod, så snart biddet nærmer sig, mens en tilredet hest tålmodigt tåler både pisk og spore. På samme måde bøjer det uciviliserede menneske ikke nakken under det åg, som det civiliserede bærer uden at klage, men foretrækker den mest stormfulde frihed frem for en fredelig underkastelse. Vi skal derfor ikke bedømme menneskets naturlige tilbøjelighed for eller imod slaveri ud fra underkuede folks fornedrelse, men ud fra de vidundere, frie folk har udrettet for at beskytte sig mod undertrykkelse. Jeg ved, at de første uafbrudt priser den fred og ro, de nyder i deres lænker, og »kalder det elendigste slaveri fred« (Tacitus, Historier, IV, 17). Men når jeg ser de andre ofre glæder, ro, rigdom, magt og selve livet for at bevare dette ene gode, som de, der har mistet det, foragter så højt; når jeg ser fritfødte dyr, der afskyr fangenskabet, knuse hovedet mod burets tremmer; og når jeg ser skarer af nøgne vilde foragte Europas nydelser og trodse sult, ild, sværd og død alene for at bevare deres uafhængighed, føler jeg, at det ikke tilkommer slaver at belære os om frihed.
reasons: Translate English-only DA slot fully against French; distinguish écrit (published work) from English edict misidentification.

danishChanges.before: With regard to paternal authority, from which some writers have derived absolute government and all society, it is enough, without going back to the contrary arguments of Locke and Sidney, to note that nothing on earth could be further from the ferocious spirit of despotism than the mildness of that authority, which looks more to the advantage of him who obeys than to that of him who commands; that by the law of nature, the father is the child's master no longer than his help is necessary; that from that time they are both equal, the son being perfectly independent of the father and owing him only respect, not obedience. For gratitude is a duty that ought to be paid, but not a right to be exacted. Instead of saying that civil society is derived from paternal authority, we ought to say rather that the latter derives its principal force from the former. No individual was ever acknowledged as the father of many until his sons and daughters settled around him. The goods of the father, of which he is really the master, are the ties that keep his children in dependence, and he may bestow on them, if he pleases, no share of his property unless they merit it by constant deference to his will. But the subjects of an arbitrary despot are so far from having any like favor to expect from their chief that they themselves and everything they possess are his property—or at least are considered by him as such—so that they are forced to receive, as a favor, the little of their own he is pleased to leave them. When he despoils them, he does but justice; and mercy, in that he permits them to live.
danishChanges.after: Hvad faderens myndighed angår, har flere afledt enevælden og hele samfundet af den. Uden at gentage Lockes og Sidneys modargumenter er det nok at bemærke, at intet i verden ligger længere fra despotismens grusomme ånd end denne myndigheds mildhed. Den tager mere hensyn til den lydendes fordel end til den befalendes. Efter naturloven er faderen kun barnets herre, så længe barnet behøver hans hjælp; derefter bliver de lige. Sønnen er da fuldstændig uafhængig af faderen og skylder ham respekt, men ikke lydighed. Taknemmelighed er ganske vist en pligt, man bør opfylde, men ikke en ret, andre kan kræve. I stedet for at sige, at det borgerlige samfund udspringer af faderens magt, burde man omvendt sige, at denne magt henter sin største styrke i samfundet. Et menneske blev først anerkendt som far til flere, da børnene blev boende samlet omkring ham. Faderens ejendom, som han virkelig råder over, er det bånd, der holder børnene afhængige af ham. Han kan lade deres andel af arven afhænge af, hvor meget de har fortjent ved stadig at rette sig efter hans vilje. Undersåtterne kan derimod ikke vente nogen lignende gunst fra deres despot. De selv og alt, hvad de ejer, tilhører ham, eller det hævder han i det mindste. Derfor må de tage imod det, han lader dem beholde af deres egen ejendom, som en nådesbevisning. Når han plyndrer dem, øver han retfærdighed; når han lader dem leve, viser han nåde.
reasons: Translate English-only DA slot fully against French; distinguish écrit (published work) from English edict misidentification.

danishChanges.before: By proceeding thus to test fact by right, we should discover as little reason as truth in the voluntary establishment of tyranny. It would also be no easy matter to prove the validity of a contract binding on only one of the parties, where all the risk is on one side and none on the other—so that no one could suffer but he who bound himself. This hateful system is indeed, even in modern times, very far from being that of wise and good monarchs, especially the kings of France, as may be seen from several passages in their edicts; particularly from the following passage in a celebrated edict published in 1667 in the name and by order of Louis XIV.
danishChanges.after: Hvis man fortsætter med således at prøve kendsgerningerne efter retten, finder man hverken holdbarhed eller sandhed i forestillingen om et frivilligt oprettet tyranni. Det ville også være svært at vise gyldigheden af en aftale, som kun forpligter den ene part, lægger alt på den ene side og intet på den anden og kun skader den, der binder sig. Denne afskyelige lære er selv i dag langt fra de kloge og gode monarkers opfattelse, især de franske kongers. Det fremgår af flere steder i deres forordninger og navnlig af følgende passage i et berømt skrift, udgivet i 1667 i Ludvig XIV's navn og på hans befaling.
reasons: Translate English-only DA slot fully against French; distinguish écrit (published work) from English edict misidentification.

danishChanges.before: "Let it not, therefore, be said that the Sovereign is not subject to the laws of his State, since the contrary is a true proposition of the right of nations, which flattery has sometimes attacked but good princes have always defended as the tutelary divinity of their dominions. How much more legitimate is it to say with the wise Plato, that the perfect felicity of a kingdom consists in the obedience of subjects to their prince, and of the prince to the laws, and in the laws being just and constantly directed to the public good!" (Of the Rights of the Most Christian Queen over various States of the Monarchy of Spain, 1667.)
danishChanges.after: »Lad derfor ingen sige, at suverænen ikke er underlagt sin stats love. Det modsatte er en sandhed i folkeretten, som smigeren undertiden har angrebet, men som gode fyrster altid har forsvaret som deres staters beskyttende guddom. Hvor meget mere berettiget er det ikke med den vise Platon at sige, at et kongeriges fuldkomne lykke består i, at undersåtterne adlyder fyrsten, at fyrsten adlyder loven, og at loven er retfærdig og altid rettet mod det fælles bedste!« (Om den aller-kristeligste dronnings rettigheder over forskellige stater under det spanske monarki, 1667.)
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation, retain Cole Barbeyrac variant and public-domain quotation; preserve qualified natural-right argument.

danishChanges.before: I will not stay here to inquire whether, since liberty is the noblest faculty of man, it is not degrading our very nature, reducing ourselves to the level of the brutes that are mere slaves of instinct, and even an affront to the Author of our being, to renounce without reserve the most precious of all His gifts, and to bow to the necessity of committing all the crimes He has forbidden, merely to gratify a mad or cruel master; or whether this sublime craftsman ought not to be less angered at seeing His workmanship entirely destroyed than thus dishonored. I will waive (if my opponents please) the authority of Barbeyrac, who, following Locke, roundly declares that no man can so far sell his liberty as to submit to an arbitrary power that may use him as it likes. For, he adds, this would be to sell his own life, of which he is not master. I will ask only what right those who were not afraid to debase themselves in this way could have to subject their posterity to the same ignominy, and to renounce for them those blessings they do not owe to the liberality of their progenitors, and without which life itself must be a burden to all who are worthy of it.
danishChanges.after: Jeg vil ikke her undersøge, om det ikke fornedrer vores natur, sænker os til dyrenes niveau som slaver af instinktet og endda krænker vores skaber, når vi uden forbehold giver afkald på friheden, den ædleste af menneskets evner og den dyrebareste af hans gaver, og underkaster os kravet om at begå alle de forbrydelser, han forbyder, blot for at behage en grusom eller vanvittig herre. Heller ikke om denne ophøjede skaber bør harmes mere over at se sit smukkeste værk ødelagt end vanæret. Hvis mine modstandere ønsker det, vil jeg også se bort fra Barbeyracs autoritet. I forlængelse af Locke erklærer han ligefrem, at intet menneske kan sælge sin frihed så fuldstændigt, at det underkaster sig en vilkårlig magt, som kan bruge det efter behag. For det ville, tilføjer han, være at sælge sit eget liv, som man ikke selv er herre over. Jeg vil blot spørge, med hvilken ret de, der ikke frygtede at fornedre sig selv så dybt, kunne underkaste deres efterkommere den samme skam og på deres vegne opgive goder, som efterkommerne ikke skylder deres forfædres gavmildhed, og uden hvilke selve livet er en byrde for enhver, der er værdig til dem.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation, retain Cole Barbeyrac variant and public-domain quotation; preserve qualified natural-right argument.

danishChanges.before: Pufendorf says that we may divest ourselves of our liberty in favor of other men, just as we transfer our property from one to another by contracts and agreements. But this seems a very weak argument. For in the first place, the property I give up becomes entirely foreign to me, and I cannot suffer from the abuse of it; but it very nearly concerns me that my liberty should not be abused, and I cannot, without incurring the guilt of the crimes I may be compelled to commit, expose myself to becoming an instrument of crime. Besides, the right of property being only a convention of human institution, men may dispose of what they possess as they please; but this is not the case with the essential gifts of nature, such as life and liberty, which every man is permitted to enjoy, and of which it is at least doubtful whether anyone has a right to divest themselves. By giving up the one, we degrade our being; by giving up the other, we do our best to annul it; and since no temporal good can compensate us for the loss of either, it would be an offense against both reason and nature to renounce them at any price whatsoever. But even if we could transfer our liberty as we do our property, there would be a great difference with regard to the children, who enjoy the father's substance only by the transmission of his right; whereas, liberty being a gift they hold from nature as men, their parents have no right whatsoever to deprive them of it. So just as to establish slavery it was necessary to do violence to nature, in order to perpetuate such a right, nature would have to be changed. Jurists, who have gravely determined that the child of a slave comes into the world a slave, have decided, in other words, that a man shall come into the world not a man.
danishChanges.after: Pufendorf siger, at ligesom man ved aftaler og kontrakter overdrager sin ejendom til andre, kan man også afgive sin frihed til fordel for nogen. Det forekommer mig at være et meget dårligt ræsonnement. For det første bliver den ejendom, jeg afhænder, mig fuldstændig uvedkommende, og dens misbrug berører mig ikke. Men det er afgørende for mig, at min frihed ikke misbruges, og jeg kan ikke udsætte mig for at blive redskab for forbrydelser uden selv at pådrage mig skyld i det onde, jeg tvinges til at gøre. Desuden beror ejendomsretten alene på aftale og menneskelige ordninger, så enhver kan råde over det, han ejer, efter eget ønske. Det samme gælder ikke naturens væsentlige gaver, som liv og frihed. Enhver må nyde dem, men det er i det mindste tvivlsomt, om nogen har ret til at give afkald på dem. Ved at opgive friheden fornedrer man sit væsen; ved at opgive livet tilintetgør man det, så vidt det står til en selv. Intet jordisk gode kan erstatte nogen af delene, så at opgive dem for nogen som helst pris ville krænke både naturen og fornuften. Men selv hvis man kunne afhænde sin frihed ligesom sin ejendom, ville der være en stor forskel for børnene. De nyder kun faderens ejendom ved at overtage hans ret, mens friheden er en gave, de har fra naturen som mennesker, og som deres forældre ingen ret har til at berøve dem. Ligesom slaveriets indførelse krævede vold mod naturen, ville en videreførelse af denne ret kræve, at naturen blev ændret. Jurister, som alvorligt har erklæret, at en slavindes barn fødes som slave, har med andre ord bestemt, at et menneske ikke skal fødes som menneske.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation, retain Cole Barbeyrac variant and public-domain quotation; preserve qualified natural-right argument.

danishChanges.before: I regard it, then, as certain that government did not begin with arbitrary power, but that this is the depravation, the extreme term, of government, and brings it back, finally, to just the law of the strongest, which it was originally designed to remedy. Even supposing it had begun in this manner, such power, being in itself illegitimate, could not have served as a basis for the laws of society, nor, consequently, for the inequality they instituted.
danishChanges.after: Det forekommer mig derfor sikkert, at regeringer ikke begyndte med vilkårlig magt. Den er tværtimod deres forfald og yderste grænse og fører dem til sidst tilbage til den stærkestes lov, som de oprindelig skulle afhjælpe. Selv hvis regeringerne var begyndt på denne måde, kunne en sådan magt, der af natur er uretmæssig, ikke have dannet grundlag for samfundets rettigheder og derfor heller ikke for den ulighed, det har indført.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation, retain Cole Barbeyrac variant and public-domain quotation; preserve qualified natural-right argument.

danishChanges.before: Without entering for now into the investigations still to be made into the nature of the fundamental compact underlying all government, I content myself with adopting the common opinion concerning it, and regard the establishment of the political body as a real contract between the people and the chiefs they have chosen—a contract by which both parties bind themselves to observe the laws therein expressed, which form the ties of their union. The people, having concentrated all their wills in one with respect to their social relations, the various articles in which this will is expressed become so many fundamental laws, binding on all the members of the state without exception. One of these articles regulates the choice and power of the magistrates appointed to watch over the execution of the rest. This power extends to everything that may maintain the constitution, without going so far as to alter it. It is accompanied by honors, in order to bring the laws and their administrators into respect. The ministers are also distinguished by personal prerogatives in order to compensate them for the cares and labor that good administration involves. The magistrate, for his part, binds himself to use the power entrusted to him only in conformity with the intention of his constituents, to maintain them all in the peaceable possession of what belongs to them, and to prefer on every occasion the public interest to his own.
danishChanges.after: Uden her at gå ind i de undersøgelser, som stadig mangler, af den grundlæggende pagt bag enhver regering, vil jeg følge den almindelige opfattelse. Jeg betragter oprettelsen af det politiske fællesskab som en virkelig kontrakt mellem folket og de ledere, det vælger. Begge parter forpligter sig til at overholde de love, kontrakten fastsætter, og som binder dem sammen. Folket har samlet alle sine viljer til én, hvad angår samfundsforholdene, og hver bestemmelse, denne vilje udtrykker, bliver en grundlov, som forpligter alle statens medlemmer uden undtagelse. En af dem regulerer valget af og magten hos de embedsmænd, der skal overvåge gennemførelsen af de øvrige. Denne magt omfatter alt, hvad der kan bevare forfatningen, men ikke det at ændre den. Til magten knyttes æresbevisninger, der skal skabe respekt for lovene og deres forvaltere, samt personlige forrettigheder, som skal kompensere embedsmændene for det krævende arbejde ved en god forvaltning. Embedsmanden forpligter sig til gengæld til kun at bruge sin betroede magt i overensstemmelse med opdragsgivernes hensigt, lade enhver nyde sin ejendom i fred og altid sætte det fælles bedste over sin egen interesse.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation, retain Cole Barbeyrac variant and public-domain quotation; preserve qualified natural-right argument.

danishChanges.before: Before experience had shown, or knowledge of the human heart enabled men to foresee, the unavoidable abuses of such a constitution, it must have appeared all the more excellent because those who were charged with the care of its preservation had themselves the most interest in it. For magistracy and the rights attaching to it being based solely on the fundamental laws, the magistrates would cease to be legitimate as soon as these ceased to exist; the people would no longer owe them obedience; and since not the magistrates but the laws are essential to the being of a state, the members of it would regain their right to their natural liberty.
danishChanges.after: Før erfaringen havde vist de uundgåelige misbrug af en sådan forfatning, eller kendskabet til menneskehjertet havde gjort det muligt at forudse dem, måtte den virke så meget bedre, fordi netop dem, der skulle bevare den, selv havde størst interesse i det. Embederne og deres rettigheder hvilede nemlig alene på grundlovene. Hvis disse ophørte med at eksistere, mistede embedsmændene deres legitimitet, og folket skyldte dem ikke længere lydighed. Da det er lovene og ikke embedsmændene, der er afgørende for statens eksistens, ville dens medlemmer genvinde retten til deres naturlige frihed.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation, retain Cole Barbeyrac variant and public-domain quotation; preserve qualified natural-right argument.

danishChanges.before: If we reflect with even a little attention on this subject, we shall find new arguments to confirm this truth, and be convinced from the very nature of the contract that it cannot be irrevocable. For if there were no superior power capable of ensuring the fidelity of the contracting parties, or compelling them to perform their reciprocal engagements, the parties would be sole judges in their own cause, and each would always have a right to renounce the contract as soon as he found that the other had violated its terms, or that they no longer suited his convenience. It is on this principle that the right of abdication may possibly be founded. Now, if, as here, we consider only what is human in this institution, it is certain that, if the magistrate, who has all the power in his own hands and appropriates all the advantages of the contract for himself, has nonetheless a right to renounce his authority, the people, who suffer for all the faults of their chief, must have a much better right to renounce their dependence. But the terrible and innumerable quarrels and disorders that would necessarily arise from so dangerous a privilege show, more than anything else, how much human governments stood in need of a more solid basis than mere reason, and how expedient it was for the public tranquility that the divine will should interpose to invest the sovereign authority with a sacred and inviolable character, which might deprive subjects of the fatal right of disposing of it. If the world had received no other advantages from religion, this would be enough to impose on men the duty of adopting and cultivating it, abuses and all, since it has been the means of saving more blood than fanaticism has ever spilt. But let us follow the thread of our hypothesis.
danishChanges.after: Overvejer vi sagen blot en smule grundigere, finder vi nye grunde til at bekræfte denne sandhed og indser af kontraktens egen natur, at den ikke kan være uigenkaldelig. Hvis der nemlig ikke findes nogen overordnet magt, som kan garantere parternes troskab eller tvinge dem til at opfylde deres gensidige forpligtelser, er de selv de eneste dommere i deres sag. Hver part har derfor altid ret til at opsige kontrakten, så snart den finder, at den anden overtræder betingelserne, eller at de ikke længere passer den. Det er måske på dette princip, retten til at abdicere kan grundlægges. Betragter vi som her kun det menneskelige ved ordningen, er det sikkert, at hvis embedsmanden, som har al magten og tilegner sig alle kontraktens fordele, alligevel har ret til at frasige sig myndigheden, må folket, som betaler for alle lederens fejl, have langt større ret til at frasige sig afhængigheden. Men de frygtelige og utallige stridigheder og uroligheder, som et så farligt privilegium nødvendigvis ville skabe, viser bedre end noget andet, hvor meget menneskers regeringer behøvede et fastere grundlag end fornuften alene. Det var afgørende for den offentlige fred, at den guddommelige vilje greb ind og gav den suveræne myndighed en hellig og ukrænkelig karakter, så undersåtterne mistede den skæbnesvangre ret til at råde over den. Selv hvis religionen ikke havde givet verden nogen anden fordel, ville dette være nok til at gøre det til en pligt at antage og dyrke den, trods dens misbrug; for den har sparet mere blod, end fanatismen har udgydt. Men lad os følge tråden i vores hypotese.
reasons: Full French-grounded DA translation, retain Cole Barbeyrac variant and public-domain quotation; preserve qualified natural-right argument.

danishChanges.before: The different forms of government owe their origin to the different degrees of inequality that existed among individuals at the time of their institution. If there happened to be any one man among them pre-eminent in power, virtue, riches, or personal influence, he became sole magistrate, and the state assumed the form of monarchy. If several, nearly equal in eminence, stood above the rest, they were elected jointly, and formed an aristocracy. Again, among a people who had deviated less from a state of nature, and between whose fortune or talents there was less disproportion, the supreme administration was retained in common, and a democracy was formed. It was discovered in time which of these forms suited men best. Some peoples remained altogether subject to the laws; others soon came to obey their magistrates. The citizens labored to preserve their liberty; the subjects, irritated at seeing others enjoying a blessing they had lost, thought only of making slaves of their neighbors. In a word, on the one side arose riches and conquests, and on the other happiness and virtue.
danishChanges.after: De forskellige regeringsformer udspringer af de større eller mindre forskelle mellem enkeltpersonerne ved oprettelsen. Var ét menneske fremragende i magt, dyd, rigdom eller indflydelse, blev han alene valgt til embedet, og staten blev et monarki. Var flere omtrent lige fremragende og hævet over resten, blev de valgt sammen, og man fik et aristokrati. De folk, hvis formuer eller evner var mindre ulige, og som havde fjernet sig mindst fra naturtilstanden, beholdt den øverste forvaltning i fællesskab og dannede et demokrati. Tiden viste, hvilken form der var mest fordelagtig for menneskene. Nogle forblev kun underlagt lovene; andre kom snart til at adlyde herrer. Borgerne ville bevare deres frihed, mens undersåtterne kun tænkte på at berøve naboerne deres, fordi de ikke kunne tåle, at andre nød et gode, de ikke længere selv havde. Kort sagt stod rigdom og erobringer på den ene side, lykke og dyd på den anden.
reasons: Full Danish translation from French/EN; preserve institutions and distinctions, explicit French seigneur etymology, note19.

danishChanges.before: In these different governments, all the offices were at first elective; and when the influence of wealth was out of the question, the preference was given to merit, which gives a natural ascendancy, and to age, which is experienced in business and deliberate in council. The Elders of the Hebrews, the Gerontes at Sparta, the Senate at Rome, and the very etymology of our word Seigneur, show how old age was once held in veneration. But the more often the choice fell upon old men, the more often elections had to be repeated, and the more they became a nuisance. Intrigues set in, factions were formed, party feeling grew bitter, civil wars broke out; the lives of individuals were sacrificed to the supposed happiness of the state; and at length men were on the point of relapsing into their primitive anarchy. Ambitious chiefs profited by these circumstances to perpetuate their offices in their own families. At the same time the people, already used to dependence, ease, and the conveniences of life, and already incapable of breaking their fetters, agreed to an increase of their slavery in order to secure their tranquility. Thus magistrates, having become hereditary, contracted the habit of regarding their offices as a family estate and themselves as proprietors of the communities of which they were at first only the officers, of treating their fellow citizens as their slaves, and counting them, like cattle, among their belongings, and of calling themselves the equals of the gods and kings of kings.
danishChanges.after: I disse forskellige regeringsformer blev alle embeder oprindeligt besat ved valg. Når rigdommen ikke var afgørende, foretrak man fortjeneste, som giver naturlig indflydelse, og alder, som giver erfaring i sagerne og ro i rådslagningen. Hebræernes ældste, Spartas geronter, Roms senat og selve oprindelsen til vores franske ord seigneur viser, hvor højt alderdommen engang blev æret. Men jo oftere valget faldt på gamle mænd, desto hyppigere måtte man vælge på ny, og desto mere mærkede man valgenes ulemper. Intriger opstod, fraktioner dannedes, partierne blev bitre, og borgerkrige brød ud. Til sidst blev borgernes blod ofret for statens påståede lykke, og man var nær ved at falde tilbage i tidligere tiders anarki. De ledendes ærgerrighed udnyttede situationen til at gøre embederne varige i deres familier. Folket var allerede vant til afhængighed, ro og livets bekvemmeligheder og kunne ikke længere bryde sine lænker. Det accepterede derfor større trældom for at sikre sin fred. Da ledernes embeder blev arvelige, vænnede de sig til at betragte dem som familieejendom og sig selv som ejere af staten, hvor de oprindeligt kun havde været embedsmænd. De kaldte deres medborgere slaver, regnede dem ligesom kvæg blandt deres ejendele og kaldte sig selv gudernes ligemænd og kongernes konger.
reasons: Full Danish translation from French/EN; preserve institutions and distinctions, explicit French seigneur etymology, note19.

danishChanges.before: If we follow the progress of inequality in these various revolutions, we shall find that the establishment of laws and of the right of property was its first stage, the institution of magistracy the second, and the conversion of legitimate into arbitrary power the third and last. So that the condition of rich and poor was authorized by the first period; that of powerful and weak by the second; and only by the third that of master and slave, which is the last degree of inequality, and the term at which all the rest remain, when they have got so far, until the government is either entirely dissolved by new revolutions, or brought back again to legitimacy.
danishChanges.after: Følger vi ulighedens udvikling gennem disse omvæltninger, finder vi, at indførelsen af loven og ejendomsretten var dens første trin, oprettelsen af embedsmyndigheden det andet og forvandlingen af legitim magt til vilkårlig magt det tredje og sidste. Den første periode gav dermed anerkendelse til forholdet mellem rig og fattig, den anden til forholdet mellem mægtig og svag og den tredje til forholdet mellem herre og slave. Dette er ulighedens sidste grad og det endepunkt, alle de andre til sidst fører til, indtil nye omvæltninger enten opløser regeringen helt eller fører den nærmere en legitim ordning igen.
reasons: Full Danish translation from French/EN; preserve institutions and distinctions, explicit French seigneur etymology, note19.

danishChanges.before: To understand this progression as necessary, we must consider not so much the motives for establishing the body politic as the forms it assumes in actuality, and the faults that necessarily attend it. For the flaws that make social institutions necessary are the same that make the abuse of them unavoidable. If we except Sparta, where the laws were mainly concerned with the education of children, and where Lycurgus established such morality as practically made laws needless—for laws, as a rule, being weaker than the passions, restrain men without altering them—it would not be difficult to prove that every government that scrupulously complied with the ends for which it was instituted, and guarded carefully against change and corruption, was set up unnecessarily. For a country in which no one either evaded the laws or made a bad use of magisterial power would need neither laws nor magistrates.
danishChanges.after: For at forstå, hvorfor denne udvikling er nødvendig, må vi se mindre på grundene til at oprette det politiske fællesskab end på den form, det faktisk antager, og de ulemper, det fører med sig. De laster, der gør samfundets ordninger nødvendige, gør nemlig også misbruget af dem uundgåeligt. Lovene er i almindelighed svagere end lidenskaberne: De holder menneskene i skak uden at forandre dem. Kun Sparta må undtages, for dér tog loven først og fremmest vare på børnenes opdragelse, og Lykurg indførte sæder, som næsten gjorde yderligere love overflødige. Det ville derfor være let at bevise, at en regering, som uden forfald eller forandring altid nøje opfyldte sit oprindelige formål, var blevet oprettet uden nødvendighed. Et land, hvor ingen omgik lovene eller misbrugte embedsmagten, ville hverken behøve embedsmænd eller love.
reasons: Full Danish translation from French/EN; preserve institutions and distinctions, explicit French seigneur etymology, note19.

danishChanges.before: Political distinctions necessarily produce civil distinctions. The growing inequality between the chiefs and the people is soon felt by individuals, and modified in a thousand ways according to passions, talents, and circumstances. The magistrate could not usurp any illegitimate power without giving distinction to the creatures with whom he must share it. Besides, individuals only allow themselves to be oppressed in so far as they are hurried on by blind ambition and, looking rather below than above them, come to love authority more than independence, and submit to slavery so that they may in turn enslave others. It is no easy matter to reduce to obedience a man who has no ambition to command; nor would the most adroit politician find it possible to enslave a people whose only desire was to be independent. But inequality easily makes its way among cowardly and ambitious minds, which are ever ready to run the risks of fortune, and almost indifferent whether they command or obey, as it is favorable or adverse. Thus there must have been a time when the eyes of the people were so dazzled that their rulers had only to say to the lowliest of men, "Be great, you and all your descendants," to make him immediately appear great in the eyes of everyone, as well as in his own. His descendants took still more upon themselves, in proportion to their distance from him; the more obscure and uncertain the cause, the greater the effect; the greater the number of idlers one could count in a family, the more illustrious it was held to be.
danishChanges.after: Politiske forskelle fører nødvendigvis til forskelle i borgernes stilling. Uligheden mellem folket og dets ledere vokser, mærkes snart mellem enkeltpersoner og antager tusind former alt efter lidenskaber, evner og omstændigheder. En embedsmand kan ikke tilrane sig uretmæssig magt uden at skabe sig tilhængere, som han må overlade en del af den til. Desuden lader borgerne sig kun undertrykke, fordi blind ærgerrighed driver dem til at se mere nedad end opad. Herredømme bliver dem kærere end uafhængighed, og de går med til selv at bære lænker for at kunne lægge dem på andre. Det er meget svært at tvinge et menneske til lydighed, hvis det ikke selv ønsker at herske, og selv den snedigste politiker kan ikke underkaste sig mennesker, som kun vil være frie. Men uligheden breder sig let blandt ærgerrige og feje sjæle, der altid er parate til at prøve lykken og næsten lige gerne hersker eller tjener, alt efter om den vender sig med eller imod dem. Der må således være kommet en tid, hvor folket var så forblændet, at dets ledere blot skulle sige til det ringeste menneske: »Vær stor, du og hele din slægt«, for at han straks forekom stor både i alles og i sine egne øjne. Hans efterkommere steg endnu højere, jo længere de kom fra ham. Jo fjernere og mere usikker årsagen var, desto større blev virkningen; jo flere lediggængere en familie kunne tælle, desto mere berømt blev den.
reasons: Full Danish translation from French/EN; preserve institutions and distinctions, explicit French seigneur etymology, note19.

danishChanges.before: If this were the place to go into details, I could readily explain how, even without the intervention of government, inequality of credit and authority became unavoidable among private persons as soon as their union in a single society made them compare themselves with one another, and take into account the differences they discovered through the continual dealings every man had to have with his neighbors. These differences are of several kinds; but riches, nobility or rank, power, and personal merit being the principal distinctions by which men form an estimate of each other in society, I could prove that the harmony or conflict of these different forces is the surest indication of the good or bad constitution of a state. I could show that among these four kinds of inequality, personal qualities being the origin of all the others, wealth is the one to which they are all reduced in the end. For, as riches tend most immediately to the prosperity of individuals and are easiest to communicate, they are used to purchase every other distinction. By this observation we are enabled to judge fairly exactly how far a people has departed from its primitive constitution, and how far it has progressed toward the extreme term of corruption. I could explain how much this universal desire for reputation, honors, and advancement, which inflames us all, exercises and holds up to comparison our faculties and powers; how it excites and multiplies our passions, and, by creating universal competition and rivalry, or rather enmity, among men, occasions countless failures, successes, and disturbances of every kind by making so many aspirants run the same course. I could show that it is to this desire to be talked about, and this unremitting rage for distinguishing ourselves, that we owe the best and the worst things we possess: both our virtues and our vices, our science and our errors, our conquerors and our philosophers—that is to say, a great many bad things and a very few good ones. In a word, I could prove that, if we have a few rich and powerful men on the pinnacle of fortune and grandeur, while the crowd grovels in want and obscurity, it is because the former prize what they enjoy only insofar as others are deprived of it; and because, without changing their condition, they would cease to be happy the moment the people ceased to be wretched.
danishChanges.after: Hvis dette var stedet at gå i detaljer, kunne jeg let forklare, hvordan ulighed i anseelse og myndighed bliver uundgåelig mellem enkeltpersoner, selv uden regeringens indgriben, [Note 19] så snart de forenes i ét samfund og dermed må sammenligne sig med hinanden og tage hensyn til de forskelle, de opdager gennem deres stadige omgang. Forskellene er af flere slags, men rigdom, adel eller rang, magt og personlig fortjeneste er de vigtigste målestokke i samfundet. Jeg kunne bevise, at samklangen eller konflikten mellem disse kræfter er det sikreste tegn på en velordnet eller dårligt indrettet stat. Jeg kunne vise, at personlige egenskaber er oprindelsen til alle de andre former for ulighed, men at de alle til sidst ender i rigdom. Den er nemlig mest umiddelbart nyttig for velbefindendet og lettest at overføre, så man kan bruge den til at købe alt det øvrige. Denne iagttagelse gør det muligt ret præcist at bedømme, hvor langt et folk har fjernet sig fra sin oprindelige ordning, og hvor langt det er nået mod det yderste forfald. Jeg kunne vise, hvor meget den almindelige trang til ry, hæder og fortrin, som fortærer os alle, udfordrer og sammenligner vores evner og kræfter; hvor meget den vækker og mangedobler lidenskaberne; og hvordan den ved at gøre alle til konkurrenter, rivaler eller snarere fjender dagligt skaber nederlag, sejre og katastrofer af enhver art, fordi så mange bejlere løber på den samme bane. Jeg kunne vise, at denne iver efter at blive omtalt og dette raseri efter at skille sig ud, som næsten altid holder os uden for os selv, har givet os både det bedste og det værste blandt mennesker: vores dyder og laster, vores videnskaber og vildfarelser, vores erobrere og filosoffer, altså mange dårlige ting og meget få gode. Kort sagt kunne jeg bevise, at når nogle få rige og mægtige står på rigdommens og storhedens tinde, mens mængden kryber i fattigdom og ubemærkethed, skyldes det, at de første kun værdsætter deres goder, fordi andre savner dem. Selv uden at deres egne vilkår ændrede sig, ville de holde op med at være lykkelige, så snart folket holdt op med at være elendigt.
reasons: Full Danish translation from French/EN; preserve institutions and distinctions, explicit French seigneur etymology, note19.

danishChanges.before: These details alone, however, would furnish matter for a considerable work, in which the advantages and disadvantages of every kind of government might be weighed as they are related to man in the state of nature; and at the same time all the different aspects under which inequality has so far appeared, or may appear in ages yet to come, according to the nature of the various governments, and the alterations time must unavoidably bring about in them, could be demonstrated. We should then see the multitude oppressed from within, in consequence of the very precautions it had taken to guard against foreign tyranny. We should see oppression continually gaining ground without its being possible for the oppressed to know where it would stop, or what legitimate means was left them of checking its progress. We should see the rights of citizens, and the freedom of nations, slowly extinguished, and the complaints, protests, and appeals of the weak treated as seditious murmurings. We should see the honor of defending the common cause confined by statecraft to a mercenary part of the people. We should see taxes made necessary by these means, and the disheartened husbandman deserting his fields even in the midst of peace, and leaving the plow to gird on the sword. We should see fatal and capricious codes of honor established, and the champions of their country sooner or later becoming its enemies, forever holding their daggers to the breasts of their fellow citizens. The time would come when they would be heard saying to the oppressor of their country:
danishChanges.after: Disse enkeltheder alene ville dog kunne fylde et stort værk, hvor man afvejede fordele og ulemper ved enhver regering i forhold til rettighederne i naturtilstanden. Her kunne man samtidig vise alle de forskellige skikkelser, uligheden hidtil har antaget og kan antage i kommende århundreder, alt efter regeringernes natur og de omvæltninger, tiden nødvendigvis vil medføre. Man ville se folkemængden blive undertrykt indefra som følge af netop de forholdsregler, den havde taget mod trusler udefra. Man ville se undertrykkelsen vokse uafbrudt, uden at de undertrykte kunne vide, hvor den ville ende, eller hvilke lovlige midler de havde tilbage til at standse den. Man ville se borgernes rettigheder og folkenes frihed langsomt slukkes og de svages klager blive behandlet som oprørsk knurren. Man ville se statskunsten begrænse æren ved at forsvare den fælles sag til en lønnet del af folket. Det ville gøre skatter nødvendige, og den modløse landmand ville selv i fredstid forlade sin mark og lægge ploven fra sig for at spænde sværdet om livet. Man ville se skæbnesvangre og besynderlige æresregler opstå. Fædrelandets forsvarere ville før eller siden blive dets fjender og altid holde dolken løftet mod deres medborgere. Til sidst ville man høre dem sige til deres lands undertrykker:
reasons: Full French-primary translation of English-only DA slot; all final philosophical argument and quotations preserved, including long p66.

danishChanges.before: "If you bid me bury my sword in my brother's breast or in my father's throat, or in the womb of my pregnant wife, I will do it all, though with reluctant hand." (Lucan, Pharsalia i, 376.)
danishChanges.after: »Befaler du mig at bore sværdet i min brors bryst, i min fars strube eller i min gravide hustrus indre, vil jeg gøre det alt sammen, selv om min hånd stritter imod.« (Lukan, Pharsalia, I, 376.)
reasons: Full French-primary translation of English-only DA slot; all final philosophical argument and quotations preserved, including long p66.

danishChanges.before: From great inequality of fortunes and conditions, from the vast variety of passions and of talents, of useless and pernicious arts, of vain sciences, would arise a multitude of prejudices equally contrary to reason, happiness, and virtue. We should see the magistrates fomenting everything that might weaken men united in society, by promoting dissension among them—everything that might sow the seeds of actual division while it gave society the air of harmony; everything that might inspire the different ranks of people with mutual hatred and distrust, by setting the rights and interests of one against those of another, and so strengthen the power that encompassed them all.
danishChanges.after: Af den yderste ulighed i stilling og formue, af lidenskabernes og evnernes mangfoldighed, af unyttige og skadelige færdigheder og tomme videnskaber ville der opstå et væld af fordomme, som stred lige meget mod fornuften, lykken og dyden. Man ville se lederne fremme alt, hvad der kunne svække forenede mennesker ved at splitte dem; alt, hvad der kunne give samfundet et ydre af enighed og samtidig så kimen til virkelig splittelse; alt, hvad der kunne indgyde de forskellige stænder mistillid og had til hinanden ved at sætte deres rettigheder og interesser op mod hinanden og dermed styrke den magt, som holdt dem alle i skak.
reasons: Full French-primary translation of English-only DA slot; all final philosophical argument and quotations preserved, including long p66.

danishChanges.before: It is out of the midst of this disorder and these revolutions that despotism, gradually raising its hideous head and devouring everything that remained sound and untainted in any part of the state, would at length trample on both the laws and the people, and establish itself on the ruins of the republic. The times immediately preceding this last change would be times of trouble and calamity; but at length the monster would swallow up everything, and the people would no longer have either chiefs or laws, but only tyrants. From this moment there would be no question of virtue or morality; for despotism—"with which there is no hope from probity"—wherever it prevails, admits no other master. No sooner does it speak than probity and duty lose their weight, and blind obedience is the only virtue slaves can still practice.
danishChanges.after: Midt i denne uorden og disse omvæltninger ville despotismen gradvis løfte sit hæslige hoved og fortære alt godt og sundt, den fandt i statens dele. Til sidst ville den træde både lovene og folket under fode og slå sig ned på republikkens ruiner. Tiden umiddelbart før denne sidste forandring ville være fuld af uro og ulykker. Men til sidst ville uhyret opsluge alt, og folkene ville ikke længere have ledere eller love, kun tyranner. Fra da af ville der heller ikke længere være tale om gode sæder eller dyd. For hvor despotismen hersker, »som intet håb har i hæderligheden«, tåler den ingen anden herre. Så snart den taler, er der hverken hæderlighed eller pligt at rådspørge; den blindeste lydighed er den eneste dyd, slaverne har tilbage.
reasons: Full French-primary translation of English-only DA slot; all final philosophical argument and quotations preserved, including long p66.

danishChanges.before: This is the last stage of inequality, the extreme point that closes the circle and meets that from which we set out. Here all private persons return to their first equality, because they are nothing; and, subjects having no law but the will of their master, and their master no restraint but his passions, all notions of good and all principles of equity again vanish. There is here a complete return to the law of the strongest, and so to a new state of nature, different from the one we set out from—for the first was a state of nature in its first purity, while this is the consequence of excessive corruption. There is so little difference between the two states in other respects, and the contract of government is so completely dissolved by despotism, that the despot is master only so long as he remains the strongest; as soon as he can be expelled, he has no right to complain of violence. The popular insurrection that ends in the death or deposition of a sultan is as lawful an act as those by which he disposed, the day before, of the lives and fortunes of his subjects. As he was maintained by force alone, it is force alone that overthrows him. Thus everything takes place according to the natural order; and whatever may be the result of such frequent and precipitate revolutions, no man has reason to complain of the injustice of another, but only of his own ill-fortune or indiscretion.
danishChanges.after: Her når uligheden sit sidste trin, det yderste punkt, som lukker kredsen og møder vores udgangspunkt. Her bliver alle enkeltpersoner igen lige, fordi de intet er. Undersåtterne har ingen anden lov end herrens vilje, og herren ingen anden regel end sine lidenskaber; derfor forsvinder forestillingerne om det gode og retfærdighedens principper igen. Alt vender tilbage til den stærkestes lov og dermed til en ny naturtilstand. Den adskiller sig fra den, vi begyndte med, ved at den første var naturtilstanden i sin renhed, mens den sidste er frugten af et yderligt forfald. Ellers er forskellen mellem de to tilstande så lille, og regeringskontrakten så fuldstændig opløst af despotismen, at despoten kun er herre, så længe han er stærkest. Så snart man kan fordrive ham, har han ingen ret til at klage over volden. Et oprør, der ender med at kvæle eller afsætte en sultan, er lige så retmæssigt som de handlinger, hvorved han dagen før rådede over sine undersåtters liv og ejendom. Kun magten holdt ham oppe, og kun magten vælter ham. Alt sker således efter naturens orden, og hvad udfaldet end bliver af disse korte og hyppige omvæltninger, kan ingen klage over andres uretfærdighed, kun over sin egen uforsigtighed eller ulykke.
reasons: Full French-primary translation of English-only DA slot; all final philosophical argument and quotations preserved, including long p66.

danishChanges.before: If the reader thus discovers and retraces the lost and forgotten road by which man must have passed from the state of nature to the state of society; if he carefully restores, along with the intermediate situations I have just described, those which want of time has compelled me to suppress, or my imagination has failed to suggest, he cannot fail to be struck by the vast distance separating the two states. It is in tracing this slow succession that he will find the solution to a number of problems of politics and morals that philosophers cannot settle. He will feel that, men being different in different ages, the reason Diogenes could not find a man was that he sought among his contemporaries a man of an earlier period. He will see that Cato died with Rome and liberty, because he did not fit the age in which he lived; the greatest of men served only to astonish a world that he would certainly have ruled, had he lived five hundred years sooner. In a word, he will explain how the soul and the passions of men insensibly change their very nature; why our needs and pleasures in the end seek new objects; and why, the original man having vanished by degrees, society offers us only an assembly of artificial men and counterfeit passions, which are the work of all these new relations, and have no real foundation in nature. We are taught nothing on this subject by reflection that is not entirely confirmed by observation. Savage and civilized man differ so much in the bottom of their hearts and in their inclinations that what constitutes the supreme happiness of one would reduce the other to despair. The former breathes only peace and liberty; he desires only to live and be free from labor; even the ataraxia of the Stoic falls far short of his profound indifference to every other object. Civilized man, on the other hand, is always moving, sweating, toiling, and racking his brains to find still more laborious occupations. He goes on drudging to his last moment, and even seeks death to put himself in a position to live, or renounces life to acquire immortality. He pays court to men in power, whom he hates, and to the wealthy, whom he despises; he stops at nothing to have the honor of serving them; he is not ashamed to value himself on his own meanness and their protection, and, proud of his slavery, he speaks with disdain of those who do not have the honor of sharing it. What a sight would the perplexing and envied labors of a European minister of state present to the eyes of a Caribbean! How many cruel deaths would not this indolent savage prefer to the horrors of such a life, which is seldom even sweetened by the pleasure of doing good! But for him to see into the motives of all this concern, the words power and reputation would have to bear some meaning in his mind; he would have to know that there are men who set a value on the opinion of the rest of the world, who can be made happy and satisfied with themselves rather on the testimony of other people than on their own. In reality, the source of all these differences is that the savage lives within himself, while social man lives constantly outside himself, and only knows how to live in the opinion of others—so that he seems to receive the consciousness of his own existence merely from the judgment of others concerning him. It is not to my present purpose to insist on the indifference to good and evil that arises from this disposition, in spite of our many fine works on morality; or to show how, with everything reduced to appearances, there is nothing but art and mummery in even honor, friendship, virtue, and often vice itself, of which we at length learn the secret of boasting; to show, in short, how, always asking others what we are, and never daring to ask ourselves, in the midst of so much philosophy, humanity, and civilization, and of such sublime codes of morality, we have nothing to show for ourselves but a frivolous and deceitful appearance—honor without virtue, reason without wisdom, and pleasure without happiness. It is enough that I have proved that this is not by any means the original state of man, but that it is merely the spirit of society, and the inequality society produces, that thus transform and alter all our natural inclinations.
danishChanges.after: Når en opmærksom læser således genfinder og følger de glemte og tabte veje, som må have ført mennesket fra naturtilstanden til samfundstilstanden, må han blive slået af den vældige afstand mellem de to. Han må til de mellemstadier, jeg har angivet, føje dem, som tidspresset har fået mig til at udelade, eller som min fantasi ikke har foreslået. I denne langsomme rækkefølge vil han finde løsningen på utallige moralske og politiske problemer, som filosofferne ikke kan løse. Han vil forstå, at menneskeslægten ikke er den samme i én tidsalder som i en anden, og at Diogenes ikke fandt et menneske, fordi han blandt sine samtidige søgte mennesket fra en tid, der ikke længere fandtes. Cato, vil han sige, gik til grunde med Rom og friheden, fordi han var malplaceret i sit århundrede. Den største af mennesker kunne kun forbløffe en verden, han ville have regeret fem hundrede år tidligere. Kort sagt vil læseren kunne forklare, hvordan menneskets sjæl og lidenskaber umærkeligt forandres og så at sige skifter natur; hvorfor vores behov og glæder med tiden søger andre genstande; og hvorfor samfundet, efterhånden som det oprindelige menneske forsvinder, kun viser den vise en samling kunstige mennesker og tillærte lidenskaber, skabt af alle disse nye forhold og uden egentligt grundlag i naturen. Det, eftertanken lærer os herom, bekræftes fuldstændigt af iagttagelsen. Det vilde og det civiliserede menneske er så forskellige i deres inderste følelser og tilbøjeligheder, at det, der gør den ene fuldkommen lykkelig, ville drive den anden til fortvivlelse. Den første ønsker kun ro og frihed, kun at leve og være ledig. Selv stoikerens ataraksi, hans sindsro, når ikke op på siden af denne dybe ligegyldighed over for alt andet. Borgeren er derimod altid aktiv: Han sveder, haster omkring og plager sig uafbrudt for at finde endnu mere krævende beskæftigelser. Han arbejder til døden og løber endda døden i møde for at skaffe sig midler til at leve eller giver afkald på livet for at vinde udødelighed. Han gør kur til de mægtige, som han hader, og de rige, som han foragter. Han skyr intet for at få æren af at tjene dem, praler stolt af sin egen kryben og deres beskyttelse og taler, stolt af sit slaveri, foragteligt om dem, der ikke har æren af at dele det. Hvilket syn ville en europæisk ministers slidsomme og misundte arbejde ikke være for en kariber! Hvor mange grusomme dødsformer ville denne magelige vilde ikke foretrække frem for rædslen ved et sådant liv, som ofte ikke engang mildnes af glæden ved at gøre godt! Men for at forstå formålet med al denne møje måtte ordene magt og anseelse have betydning for ham. Han måtte lære, at der findes mennesker, som lægger vægt på resten af verdens blik og kan være lykkelige og tilfredse med sig selv på grundlag af andres vidnesbyrd snarere end deres eget. Her ligger den egentlige årsag til alle forskellene: Den vilde lever i sig selv; samfundsmennesket lever altid uden for sig selv og kun gennem andres mening. Det er så at sige alene fra deres dom, at det henter følelsen af sin egen eksistens. Det er ikke mit emne her at vise, hvordan denne indstilling skaber så megen ligegyldighed over for godt og ondt trods alle de smukke moralske taler; hvordan alt bliver kunstigt og spillet, når det kun handler om at tage sig ud: ære, venskab, dyd og ofte selv lasterne, som man til sidst lærer at prale af. Heller ikke hvordan vi altid spørger andre, hvem vi er, og aldrig vover at spørge os selv, så vi midt i al vores filosofi, menneskelighed, dannelse og ophøjede grundsætninger kun har et bedragerisk og overfladisk ydre: ære uden dyd, fornuft uden visdom og nydelse uden lykke. Det er nok, at jeg har vist, at dette på ingen måde er menneskets oprindelige tilstand, og at kun samfundets ånd og den ulighed, det frembringer, ændrer og forvansker alle vores naturlige tilbøjeligheder på denne måde.
reasons: Full French-primary translation of English-only DA slot; all final philosophical argument and quotations preserved, including long p66.

danishChanges.before: I have endeavored to trace the origin and progress of inequality, and the institution and abuse of political societies, so far as these can be deduced from the nature of man merely by the light of reason, and independently of those sacred dogmas that give the sanction of divine right to sovereign authority. It follows from this survey that, since there is hardly any inequality in the state of nature, all the inequality that now prevails owes its strength and growth to the development of our faculties and the advance of the human mind, and becomes at last permanent and legitimate by the establishment of property and laws. Secondly, it follows that moral inequality, authorized by positive right alone, clashes with natural right whenever it is not proportionate to physical inequality—a distinction that sufficiently determines what we ought to think of that species of inequality which prevails in all civilized countries; since it is plainly contrary to the law of nature, however defined, that children should command old men, fools wise men, and that the privileged few should gorge themselves on superfluities, while the starving multitude lack the bare necessities of life.
danishChanges.after: Jeg har forsøgt at fremstille ulighedens oprindelse og udvikling og de politiske samfunds oprettelse og misbrug, så vidt disse forhold kan udledes af menneskets natur ved fornuftens lys alene og uafhængigt af de hellige læresætninger, som giver den suveræne myndighed guddommelig ret. Af fremstillingen følger, at uligheden, som næsten ikke findes i naturtilstanden, får sin styrke og vækst fra udviklingen af vores evner og menneskeåndens fremskridt og til sidst bliver fast og legitim gennem ejendommens og lovenes indførelse. Det følger også, at moralsk ulighed, som kun er godkendt af den fastsatte ret, strider mod naturretten, hver gang den ikke står i samme forhold til den fysiske ulighed. Denne skelnen er tilstrækkelig til at afgøre, hvad vi skal mene om den ulighed, der hersker blandt alle civiliserede folk. For det strider åbenlyst mod naturloven, hvordan man end definerer den, at et barn skal befale over en olding, at en tåbe skal lede et klogt menneske, og at en håndfuld mennesker skal svælge i overflod, mens den sultende mængde mangler det nødvendige.

englishChanges.before: I would have wished, then, that no one inside the state could claim to be above the law, and that no outsider could dictate terms the state was forced to recognize. For whatever a government's constitution may be, if a single person within its jurisdiction is not subject to the law, all the rest are necessarily at his mercy. And if there is a national ruler inside and a foreign ruler outside, however they divide their authority, it is impossible for both to be properly obeyed or for the state to be well governed.
englishChanges.after: I would have wished, then, that no one inside the state could claim to be above the law, and that no outsider could dictate terms the state was forced to recognize. And if there is a national ruler inside and a foreign ruler outside, however they divide their authority, it is impossible for both to be properly obeyed or for the state to be well governed. [Author’s note 1: Herodotus relates that after the killing of the false Smerdis, the seven liberators of Persia met to discuss the form of government they would give the state. Otanes argued strongly for a republic. This was all the more extraordinary coming from a satrap, since he could himself lay claim to the throne, and the great fear a government that forces them to respect other people more than they fear death. As one might expect, Otanes was not heard. Seeing that they were about to elect a monarch, he, who wished neither to obey nor to command, voluntarily surrendered his claim to the crown to the other contenders. As his sole compensation he asked that he and his descendants should be free and independent, and this was granted. Even if Herodotus had not told us of the restriction placed on this privilege, we would necessarily have to suppose one. Otherwise Otanes, acknowledging no law and accountable to nobody, would have been all-powerful in the state and more powerful than the king himself. Yet it was hardly likely that a man capable of being content with such a privilege in such circumstances would abuse it. Indeed, there is no indication that this right ever caused the slightest disturbance in the kingdom, either through the wise Otanes or through any of his descendants.]
