englishChanges.before: It should not be surprising that the rulers of a civil society have the welfare and glory of their communities at heart. But it is uncommonly fortunate for the peace of mankind when those who consider themselves the magistrates—or rather the masters—of a holier and more sublime country show some love for the earthly country that sustains them. I am happy to make so singular an exception in our favor, and to be able to rank, among its best citizens, those zealous keepers of the sacred articles of faith established by the laws, those venerable shepherds of souls whose powerful and engaging eloquence is all the better suited to carry the maxims of the gospel into people's hearts because they themselves are the first to put them into practice. Everyone knows how successfully the art of preaching is cultivated in Geneva. But people are so used to hearing clergymen preach one thing and practice another that few have any way of knowing how far the spirit of Christianity, holiness of conduct, severity toward themselves, and indulgence toward their neighbors actually prevail throughout the whole body of our ministers. It is perhaps given to the city of Geneva alone to produce the edifying example of so perfect a union between its clergy and its men of letters. It is largely on their wisdom, their well-known moderation, and their zeal for the state's prosperity that I build my hopes for its lasting tranquility. At the same time, I notice with pleasure mixed with surprise and reverence how thoroughly they reject the dreadful maxims of those accursed and barbarous men of whom history furnishes more than one example—men who, in order to defend the supposed rights of God (meaning their own interests), have been all the less sparing of human blood the more confident they were that their own, in particular, would always be respected.

englishChanges.before: I must not forget that precious half of the republic which makes the happiness of the other, and whose sweetness and prudence preserve its tranquility and virtue. Amiable and virtuous daughters of Geneva, it will always be your sex's lot to govern ours. Happy are we, so long as your chaste influence, exercised only within the bounds of marriage, is exerted for the glory of the state and the happiness of the public. It was this way that women commanded at Sparta, and this is how you deserve to command at Geneva. What man can be such a barbarian as to resist the voice of honor and reason coming from the lips of an affectionate wife? Who would not despise the vanities of luxury, on seeing the simple and modest dress which, lit by the radiance it borrows from you, seems most flattering to beauty? Your task is to perpetuate, by your gentle influence and your innocent and amiable rule, respect for the laws of the state and harmony among the citizens. It is yours to reunite divided families by happy marriages and, above all, to correct, by the persuasive sweetness of your lessons and the modest grace of your conversation, the extravagances our young people pick up in other countries—where, instead of the many useful things they could profit by, they bring home hardly anything besides a childish swagger and a ridiculous manner picked up among loose women, plus an admiration for some so-called grandeur and paltry rewards for being slaves, which can never come anywhere near the real greatness of liberty. Continue, then, always to be what you are, the chaste guardians of our morals and the sweet pledge of our peace, exerting on every occasion the privileges of the heart and of nature in the service of duty and virtue.

englishChanges.before: Of all human sciences, the most useful and the most imperfect, in my view, is the one that studies humankind. I will venture to say that the single inscription on the Temple of Delphi contained a precept more difficult and more important than anything in all the huge volumes the moralists have ever written. I consider the subject of this discourse one of the most interesting questions philosophy can propose, and unfortunately for us, one of the thorniest philosophers have to solve. For how can we know the source of inequality among human beings if we don't first know what human beings are? And how can a person hope to see himself as nature made him, through all the changes that the succession of times and circumstances must have produced in his original constitution? How can he distinguish what is fundamental to his nature from the changes and additions his circumstances and his progress have introduced into his primitive condition? Like the statue of Glaucus—so disfigured by time, sea, and storms that it looked more like a wild beast than a god—the human soul, altered in society by a thousand constantly recurring causes, by the acquisition of countless truths and errors, by changes in the body's constitution, and by the continual collision of the passions, has, so to speak, changed in appearance to the point of being almost unrecognizable. Instead of a being acting always from fixed and unchanging principles, instead of that heavenly and majestic simplicity its divine Author impressed on it, we now find only the deformed contrast of passion mistaking itself for reason, and of an understanding gone delirious.

Instead of a being acting always from fixed and unchanging principles, instead of that heavenly and majestic simplicity its divine Author impressed on it, we now find only the deformed contrast of passion mistaking itself for reason, and of an understanding gone delirious. [Author’s note 2: At my very first step I rely confidently on one of those authorities that philosophers must respect because they spring from a sound and elevated reason that only they know how to discover and appreciate. “However interested we may be in knowing ourselves, I wonder whether we do not know everything else better. Equipped by nature with organs intended solely for our preservation, we use them only to receive impressions from outside; we seek only to extend ourselves outward and to exist outside ourselves. Too occupied with multiplying the functions of our senses and enlarging the outward extent of our being, we rarely use that inward sense which reduces us to our true dimensions and separates from us everything that is not ourselves. Yet this is the sense we must use if we wish to know ourselves; it is the only one through which we can judge ourselves. But how can we give this sense its activity and full scope? How can we free our soul, in which it resides, from all the illusions of our understanding? We have lost the habit of using it; it has remained unexercised amid the tumult of our bodily sensations and has been dried out by the fire of our passions. Heart, understanding, senses—everything has worked against it.” _Natural History_, vol. 4, p. 151, “On Human Nature.”]

englishChanges.before: A DISCOURSE
englishChanges.after:
_Question proposed by the Academy of Dijon_

What is the origin of inequality among people, and is it authorized by natural law?

_Author’s notice on the notes_

I have added some notes to this work, following my lazy habit of working in fits and starts. These notes sometimes wander too far from the subject to be read alongside the text. I have therefore placed them at the end of the discourse, in which I have tried to follow the most direct path as well as I could. Those with the courage to begin again may amuse themselves on a second reading by exploring the byways and attempting the notes; little harm will be done if the others do not read them at all.

A DISSERTATION
reasons: Restore Academy question and complete French author notice explaining separate endnotes, absent from corpus

englishChanges.before: But even if the difficulties surrounding all these questions still left some room for disagreement on this point between men and beasts, there is another very specific quality that distinguishes them and admits no dispute: the faculty of self-improvement, which, with the help of circumstances, gradually develops all our other faculties, and which is inherent in the species as in the individual. A beast, at the end of a few months, is all that it will ever be during its whole life, and its species, at the end of a thousand years, is exactly what it was in the first year of those thousand. Why is man alone subject to growing into a doddering old fool? Is it not because he is, in this, returning to his primitive state—and that whereas the beast, which has acquired nothing and therefore has nothing to lose, still retains the force of instinct, man, who loses, through age or accident, all that his perfectibility had enabled him to gain, falls thereby even lower than the beasts themselves? It would be a melancholy thing if we were forced to admit that this distinctive and almost unlimited faculty is the source of all human misfortunes; that it is this that, in time, draws man out of his original condition, in which he would have spent his days insensibly in peace and innocence; that it is this faculty that, by successively producing in different ages his discoveries and his errors, his vices and his virtues, makes him at length a tyrant both over himself and over nature. It would be shocking to be obliged to regard as a benefactor the man who first suggested to the Orinoco Indians the use of those boards they apply to the temples of their children, which secure to them at least some part of their imbecility and original happiness.

englishChanges.before: Savage man, left by nature to the sole guidance of instinct—or rather compensated for what he lacks by faculties capable at first of replacing it and later of raising him much above it—must accordingly begin with purely animal functions. Seeing and feeling must be his first condition, which he would share with all other animals. To will and not to will, to desire and to fear, must be the first and almost the only operations of his soul, until new circumstances cause new developments of his faculties.

englishChanges.before: Whatever moralists may say, the human understanding owes much to the passions, which, it is universally allowed, also owe much to the understanding. It is by the activity of the passions that our reason is improved, for we desire knowledge only because we wish to enjoy, and it is impossible to imagine why a person who has neither fears nor desires should bother to reason at all. The passions, in turn, originate in our needs, and their progress depends on that of our knowledge—for we can only desire or fear something on the basis of the idea we have of it, or from the simple impulse of nature. Now savage man, destitute of every kind of intelligence, can have no passions except those of the latter sort: his desires never go beyond his physical needs. The only goods he recognizes in the universe are food, a female, and sleep; the only evils he fears are pain and hunger. I say pain, not death, because no animal can know what it is to die: the knowledge of death and its terrors is one of the first things man acquires on departing from an animal state.

englishChanges.before: Above all, let us not conclude, with Hobbes, that because man has no idea of goodness, he must be naturally wicked; that he is vicious because he doesn't know virtue; that he always refuses to do his fellow creatures services he doesn't think they have a right to demand; or that by virtue of the right he rightly claims to everything he needs, he foolishly imagines himself the sole proprietor of the whole universe. Hobbes had seen clearly the defects of all the modern definitions of natural right; but the consequences he draws from his own show that he understands it in an equally false sense. Reasoning on the principles he lays down, he ought to have said that the state of nature, being the one in which the care for our own preservation is least prejudicial to that of others, was consequently best calculated to promote peace, and the most suitable for mankind. He says the exact opposite, because he has improperly included, as part of savage man's care for his self-preservation, the gratification of a multitude of passions that are the work of society and have made laws necessary. A bad man, he says, is a robust child. But it remains to be proved that man in a state of nature is this robust child; and even if we granted that he is, what would he infer? Why, truly, that if this man, when robust and strong, were dependent on others as he is when feeble, there is no extravagance he would not be guilty of: that he would beat his mother when she was too slow in giving him her breast; that he would strangle one of his younger brothers if he found him troublesome; or that he would bite another's arm if he caused him any inconvenience. But that man in the state of nature is both strong and dependent involves two contrary suppositions. Man is weak when he is dependent, and is his own master before he comes to be strong. Hobbes did not reflect that the same cause that prevents a savage from making use of his reason (as our jurists hold) prevents him also from abusing his faculties (as Hobbes himself allows). So it may be justly said that savages are not bad merely because they don't know what it is to be good: for it is neither the development of the understanding nor the restraint of law that hinders them from doing ill, but the peacefulness of their passions and their ignorance of vice—"so much more does the ignorance of vice profit the one sort than the knowledge of virtue the other." There is another principle that escaped Hobbes, which, having been bestowed on mankind to moderate, on certain occasions, the impetuosity of egoism, or, before its birth, the desire of self-preservation, tempers the ardor with which he pursues his own welfare by an innate repugnance at seeing a fellow creature suffer. I do not think I need fear contradiction in holding that man is endowed with the only natural virtue that not even the most violent detractor of human virtue could deny him. I am speaking of compassion, a disposition suited to creatures as weak and subject to so many ills as we certainly are—all the more universal and useful to mankind because it comes before any kind of reflection, and at the same time so natural that the very beasts themselves sometimes give clear proofs of it. Not to mention the tenderness of mothers for their young and the perils they brave to save them from danger, it is well known that horses are reluctant to trample on living bodies; one animal never passes by the dead body of another of its species; there are even some that give their fellows a sort of burial; and the mournful lowing of cattle as they enter the slaughterhouse shows the impressions made on them by the horrible spectacle that meets them. We find, with pleasure, the author of the Fable of the Bees obliged to admit that man is a compassionate and sensitive being, and laying aside his cold subtle style, in the example he gives, to present us with the pathetic description of a man who, from a place of confinement, is forced to behold a wild beast tear a child from the arms of its mother, crushing its tender limbs with its murderous teeth, and tearing its quivering entrails with its claws. What horrid agitation must not the eyewitness of such a scene experience, even though he were not personally involved! What anxiety would he not suffer at not being able to give any help to the fainting mother and the dying infant!

englishChanges.before: Such is the pure emotion of nature, prior to all reflection! Such is the force of natural compassion, which the greatest depravity of morals has so far hardly been able to destroy! For every day at our theaters we see men moved—even brought to tears—by the sufferings of a wretch who, were he in the tyrant's place, would probably even add to the torments of his enemies; like the bloodthirsty Sulla, who was so sensitive to ills he had not caused, or that Alexander of Pherae who didn't dare go and see any tragedy performed, for fear of being seen weeping with Andromache and Priam, though he could listen without emotion to the cries of all the citizens who were daily strangled at his command.

englishChanges.before: Mandeville well knew that, despite all their morality, men would never have been any better than monsters had nature not bestowed on them a sense of compassion to assist their reason. But he did not see that from this quality alone flow all those social virtues he denied man any possession of. For what is generosity, clemency, or humanity but compassion applied to the weak, the guilty, or to mankind in general? Even benevolence and friendship, if we judge rightly, are only the effects of compassion constantly directed at a particular object: for how is it different to wish that another person should not suffer pain and uneasiness, and to wish him happy? Even if it were true that pity is no more than a feeling that puts us in the place of the sufferer—a feeling obscure yet lively in a savage, developed yet feeble in civilized man—this truth would have no other consequence than to confirm my argument. Compassion must, in fact, be the stronger the more the animal beholding any kind of distress identifies himself with the animal that suffers. Now, it is plain that such identification must have been much more complete in a state of nature than in a state of reason. It is reason that generates self-respect, and reflection that confirms it. It is reason that turns the human mind back on itself and divides him from everything that could disturb or afflict him. It is philosophy that isolates him and bids him say, at the sight of the misfortunes of others, "Perish if you will, I am safe." Nothing but such general evils as threaten the whole community can disturb the tranquil sleep of the philosopher or tear him from his bed. A murder may be committed under his window with impunity; he has only to put his hands over his ears and argue a little with himself to prevent nature, which is shocked within him, from identifying itself with the unfortunate sufferer. Uncivilized man has no such admirable talent, and for lack of reason and wisdom is always foolishly ready to obey the first promptings of humanity. It is the populace that crowds together at riots and street brawls, while the wise man prudently makes off. It is the mob and the market women who part the combatants, and prevent gentlefolk from cutting each other's throats.

englishChanges.before: It is therefore certain that compassion is a natural feeling that, by moderating the violence of love of self in each individual, contributes to the preservation of the whole species. It is this compassion that hurries us, without reflection, to the relief of those in distress; it is this that, in a state of nature, takes the place of laws, morals, and virtues, with the advantage that no one is tempted to disobey its gentle voice; it is this that will always prevent a strong savage from robbing a weak child or a feeble old man of the sustenance they may have acquired with pain and difficulty, so long as he sees a way of providing for himself by other means; it is this that, instead of inculcating the sublime maxim of rational justice, "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you," inspires all men with that other maxim of natural goodness—much less perfect indeed, but perhaps more useful: "Do good to yourself with as little harm as possible to others." In short, it is in this natural feeling rather than in any subtle arguments that we must look for the cause of that aversion every man would feel toward doing evil, even independently of the maxims of education. Although it might belong to Socrates and other minds of the same craft to acquire virtue by reason, the human race would long since have ceased to exist if its preservation had depended only on the reasonings of the individuals who composed it.

englishChanges.before: With passions so little active, and so good a check on them, men, being rather wild than wicked and more intent on guarding themselves against the harm that might be done to them than on doing harm to others, were by no means subject to very dangerous dissensions. They had no kind of dealings with one another, and were consequently strangers to vanity, deference, esteem, and contempt. They had not the least idea of mine and thine, and no true conception of justice. They looked on every act of violence they were subjected to as an injury easily repaired, rather than as a crime deserving punishment, and they never thought of taking revenge unless perhaps mechanically and on the spot, as a dog will sometimes bite the stone thrown at him. Their quarrels would therefore seldom have very bloody consequences, since the subject of them would be merely a question of subsistence. But I am aware of one greater danger, which remains to be noticed.

englishChanges.before: Men in a state of nature, confined merely to what is physical in love, and fortunate enough to be ignorant of those refinements that whet the appetite while increasing the difficulty of gratifying it, must be subject to fewer and less violent fits of passion, and consequently fall into fewer and less violent disputes. The imagination, which causes such ravages among us, never speaks to the heart of savages, who quietly await the impulses of nature, yield to them involuntarily, with more pleasure than ardor, and, their needs once satisfied, lose the desire. It is therefore beyond dispute that love, like all other passions, must have acquired in society the glowing impetuosity that makes it so often fatal to mankind. And it is all the more absurd to picture savages as continually cutting one another's throats to indulge their brutality, because this opinion is directly contrary to experience. The Caribs, who have so far departed least of all from the state of nature, are in fact the most peaceable people in their loves, and the least subject to jealousy, even though they live in a hot climate that always seems to inflame the passions.
englishChanges.after: Men in a state of nature, confined merely to what is physical in love, and fortunate enough to be ignorant of those refinements that whet the appetite while increasing the difficulty of gratifying it, must be subject to fewer and less violent fits of passion, and consequently fall into fewer and less violent disputes. The imagination, which causes such ravages among us, never speaks to the heart of savages, who quietly await the impulses of nature, yield to them without preferring a particular partner, with more pleasure than ardor, and, their needs once satisfied, lose the desire. It is therefore beyond dispute that love, like all other passions, must have acquired in society the glowing impetuosity that makes it so often fatal to mankind. And it is all the more absurd to picture savages as continually cutting one another's throats to indulge their brutality, because this opinion is directly contrary to experience. The Caribs, who have so far departed least of all from the state of nature, are in fact the most peaceable people in their loves, and the least subject to jealousy, even though they live in a hot climate that always seems to inflame the passions.
reasons: French sans choix concerns lack of selective preference, not involuntary action.

englishChanges.before: Such was the condition of infant man: the life of an animal, limited at first to mere sensations, hardly profiting from the gifts nature bestowed on him, much less capable of entertaining the thought of forcing anything from her. But difficulties soon presented themselves, and it became necessary to learn to overcome them. The height of the trees, which prevented him from gathering their fruits; the competition of other animals desiring the same fruits; and the ferocity of those who needed them for their own preservation—all this obliged him to apply himself to physical exercises. He had to become active, swift of foot, and vigorous in the fight. Natural weapons—stones and sticks—were easily found. He learned to overcome nature's obstacles, to fight when necessary with other animals, and to dispute the means of subsistence even with other men, or to make up for what he was forced to give up to a stronger one.

englishChanges.before: Other men, it is true, were not then to him what they are now to us, and he had no greater dealings with them than with other animals; yet they were not left out of his observations. The conformities he would in time discover between them, and between himself and his female, led him to judge of others not yet perceptible. Finding that they all behaved as he himself would have done in like circumstances, he naturally inferred that their manner of thinking and acting was entirely in conformity with his own. This important truth, once deeply impressed on his mind, must have induced him, by an intuitive feeling more certain and far quicker than any kind of reasoning, to follow the rules of conduct he had best observe toward them for his own security and advantage.

englishChanges.before: These first advances enabled men to make others more rapidly. As they grew more enlightened, they grew more industrious. They stopped falling asleep under the first tree or in the first cave that offered them shelter; they invented several kinds of implements out of hard, sharp stones, which they used to dig the earth and cut wood. They then made huts out of branches, and afterward learned to plaster them with mud and clay. This was the epoch of a first revolution, which established and distinguished families and introduced a kind of property—itself the source of a thousand quarrels and conflicts. Since the strongest were probably the first to build themselves huts they felt able to defend, it may be concluded that the weak found it much easier and safer to imitate them than to try to dislodge them. And among those already provided with huts, no one could have any incentive to take possession of his neighbor's—not so much because it didn't belong to him as because it could be of no use to him, and he could not seize it without exposing himself to a desperate battle with the family that occupied it.

englishChanges.before: As ideas and feelings succeeded one another, and heart and mind were brought into play, men continued to lay aside their original wildness. Their private connections grew more intimate every day as their boundaries extended. They got into the habit of gathering before their huts around a large tree; singing and dancing—the true offspring of love and leisure—became the amusement, or rather the occupation, of men and women thus assembled together with nothing else to do. Each one began to look at the rest, and to want to be looked at in turn; and so a value came to be attached to public esteem. Whoever sang or danced best, whoever was the handsomest, the strongest, the most skillful, or the most eloquent, came to be the most regarded. This was the first step toward inequality and, at the same time, toward vice. From these first distinctions arose, on the one hand, vanity and contempt, and on the other, shame and envy; and the fermentation caused by these new yeasts ended in producing combinations fatal to innocence and happiness.

englishChanges.before: Behold, then, all human faculties developed, memory and imagination in full play, egoism interested, reason active, and the mind almost at the highest point of its perfection. Behold all the natural qualities in action: the rank and condition of every man assigned him; not only his share of property and his power to serve or injure others, but also his wit, beauty, strength or skill, merit or talents. And these being the only qualities capable of commanding respect, it soon became necessary to possess them or to pretend to.

englishChanges.before: It now became the interest of men to appear what they really were not. To be and to seem became two totally different things; and from this distinction sprang insolent pomp and cheating trickery, with all the numerous vices that go in their train. On the other hand, free and independent as men had been before, they were now, in consequence of a multitude of new wants, brought into subjection, as it were, to all nature, and especially to one another. Each became in some degree a slave even in becoming the master of other men. If rich, they needed others' services; if poor, others' help; and even a middling condition did not enable them to do without one another. Man must now, therefore, have been perpetually employed in getting others to interest themselves in his lot, and in making them, apparently at least if not really, find their advantage in promoting his own. He must therefore have been sly and artful in his behavior to some, and imperious and cruel to others, being under a kind of necessity to ill-use all the people he needed when he could not frighten them into compliance and did not judge it his interest to be useful to them. Insatiable ambition, the thirst to raise their respective fortunes—not so much out of real need as from the desire to outdo others—inspired all men with a vile inclination to harm one another, and with a secret jealousy which is all the more dangerous because it puts on the mask of benevolence to carry its point with greater security. In short, there arose rivalry and competition on the one hand, and conflicting interests on the other, together with a secret desire on both sides to profit at the expense of others. All these evils were the first effects of property, and the inseparable attendants of growing inequality.

englishChanges.before: Before the invention of signs to represent riches, wealth could hardly consist in anything but lands and cattle—the only real possessions men can have. But when inheritances increased in number and extent until they covered the whole of the land and bordered on one another, one man could only enlarge himself at another's expense. At the same time, the supernumeraries, who had been too weak or too lazy to make such acquisitions, and had grown poor without sustaining any loss—because while they saw everything change around them, they themselves remained the same—were obliged to receive their subsistence, or steal it, from the rich. And this soon bred, according to their different characters, either dominion and slavery, or violence and pillage. The wealthy, for their part, had no sooner begun to taste the pleasure of command than they disdained all others; and, using their old slaves to acquire new ones, they thought of nothing but subduing and enslaving their neighbors, like ravenous wolves which, having once tasted human flesh, despise every other food and from then on seek only men to devour.

englishChanges.before: It is impossible that men should not at length have reflected on so wretched a situation, and on the calamities that overwhelmed them. The rich, in particular, must have felt how much they suffered by a constant state of war, of which they bore all the expense, and in which, though all risked their lives, they alone risked their property. Besides, however speciously they might disguise their usurpations, they knew they were founded on precarious and false titles, so that if others took from them by force what they themselves had gained by force, they would have no reason to complain. Even those who had been enriched by their own industry could hardly base their proprietorship on better claims. It was in vain to repeat: "I built this well; I gained this spot by my industry." "Who gave you your standing?" it might be answered. "And what right have you to demand payment of us for doing what we never asked you to do? Do you not know that countless others of your fellow creatures are starving for want of what you have too much of? You ought to have had the express and universal consent of mankind before appropriating more of the common subsistence than you needed for your own maintenance." englishChanges.before: This is the last stage of inequality, the extreme point that closes the circle and meets that from which we set out. Here all private persons return to their first equality, because they are nothing; and, subjects having no law but the will of their master, and their master no restraint but his passions, all notions of good and all principles of equity again vanish. There is here a complete return to the law of the strongest, and so to a new state of nature, different from the one we set out from—for the first was a state of nature in its first purity, while this is the consequence of excessive corruption. There is so little difference between the two states in other respects, and the contract of government is so completely dissolved by despotism, that the despot is master only so long as he remains the strongest; as soon as he can be expelled, he has no right to complain of violence. onboardingChanges.before:
Afhandling om ulighedens oprindelse og grundlag blandt menneskene stiller et spørgsmål, der lyder simpelt og viser sig at være sprængfarligt: hvor kommer ulighed fra? Rousseaus svar er, at naturlig ulighed — forskelle i styrke eller intelligens — er ubetydelig sammenlignet med den moralske og politiske ulighed, som civilisationen skaber. Han konstruerer en spekulativ historie om menneskeslægten fra en ensom, selvtilstrækkelig naturtilstand gennem opfindelsen af ejendom, landbrug og regering, og hævder, at hvert skridt gjorde mennesker mere afhængige af hinanden og mere ulige. Den berømte linje — »Det første menneske, der, efter at have indhegnet et stykke jord, fik den idé at sige dette er mit, og fandt folk enfoldige nok til at tro ham, var det borgerlige samfunds sande grundlægger« — fanger argumentets kraft.

Skrevet i 1754 som svar på et prisspørgsmål fra Akademiet i Dijon og udgivet i 1755 er Afhandlingen en af den moderne politiske filosofis grundtekster. Den brød med Voltaires og filosoffernes oplysningsoptimisme ved at hævde, at civilisationen ikke havde forbedret menneskeheden, men fordærvet den — at kunsterne, videnskaberne og de samfundsinstitutioner, oplysningstiden hyldede, netop var ulighedens og afhængighedens mekanismer. Argumentet påvirkede den franske revolution, den romantiske filosofi, Marx' redegørelse for fremmedgørelse og enhver senere kritik af fremskridtet, der spørger, om moderniteten har gjort mennesker friere eller mere gennemgribende kontrolleret.
onboardingChanges.after:
Hvor kommer forskellene i rigdom, magt og anseelse fra? Rousseau skelner mellem naturlige forskelle, som alder og styrke, og den moralske eller politiske ulighed, der opstår gennem menneskers aftaler og samfundsordninger. Han undersøger, hvordan ejendom, arbejdsdeling og afhængighed kan gøre forskellene større.

Værket fra 1755 består her af en tilegnelse til Genève, et forord og to hoveddele. Første del undersøger et tænkt menneske før samfundslivet; anden del følger udviklingen mod ejendom, regering og vilkårlig magt. Rousseau understreger, at hans fremstilling bygger på antagelser, ikke på en dokumenteret beretning om menneskehedens fortid. Noterne uddyber argumenterne og diskuterer blandt andre Hobbes og Locke.

before.title: Naturtilstanden — tankeeksperiment eller historie?
before.text: Rousseau beskriver et ensomt, fredeligt naturmenneske, der næsten intet behøver og ikke afhænger af nogen. Han insisterer på, at dette ikke er historie, men et redskab til at måle, hvor langt civilisationen har ført os fra vores oprindelige tilstand. Læg mærke til, hvor han behandler det som hypotetisk, og hvor han synes at tro på det.
before.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse Afhandlingen som et tankeeksperiment om den menneskelige natur — forstå, hvad Rousseau mener, vi var, før samfundet formede os, og om hans »naturmenneske« er en virkelig påstand eller et filosofisk redskab.

before.title: Ejendom som al ondskabs oprindelse.
before.text: Rousseaus mest radikale påstand: opfindelsen af privat ejendom er det øjeblik, hvor alt går galt. Før ejendom var ulighed ubetydelig. Efter den følger enhver form for herredømme. Følg, hvordan han bygger sagen op — og om den overbeviser.
before.angleObjective: Jeg vil følge Rousseaus argument om, at privat ejendom er roden til politisk ulighed — se præcis, hvordan han forbinder indhegningens handling med slaveri, krig og staten.

before.title: Medfølelse før fornuft.
before.text: Rousseau hævder, at naturmennesket har to grunddrifter: selvopholdelse og medlidenhed — en naturlig modvilje mod at se andre lide. Fornuften kommer senere og svækker faktisk medfølelsen. Denne omvending af oplysningstidens rangorden er en af de mest provokerende påstande i teksten.
before.angleObjective: Jeg vil spore Rousseaus påstand om, at medfølelse er mere grundlæggende end fornuft — at medlidenhed er naturlig, mens refleksion er en fordærvelse — og afprøve den mod mine egne intuitioner om, hvad der gør mennesker moralske.

before.title: Imod fremskridtet.
before.text: Oplysningstiden sagde, at civilisationen forbedrer menneskeheden. Rousseau sagde, at den slavebinder os. Afhandlingen er det første systematiske argument for, at fremskridtet ikke er, hvad det giver sig ud for at være — at ethvert fremskridt i viden, teknologi og samfundsorganisation er sket på bekostning af frihed og lighed.
before.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse Afhandlingen som den grundlæggende kritik af fremskridtet — Rousseaus sag for, at civilisationen har gjort os mere afhængige, mere ulige og mindre frie — og afgøre, hvor meget af den der stadig holder.

after.title: Hvad er naturligt?
after.text: Rousseau vil skelne mellem det, mennesket har fra naturen, og det, livet blandt andre har gjort det til. Følg hans antagelser om det oprindelige menneske.
after.angleObjective: Jeg vil undersøge, hvad Rousseaus naturtilstand skal forklare, og hvilke antagelser forklaringen afhænger af.

after.title: Ejendom og afhængighed
after.text: Jord, arbejdsdeling og fælles regler forandrer forholdet mellem mennesker. Læg mærke til de mellemtrin, der forbinder besiddelse med politisk magt.
after.angleObjective: Jeg vil følge argumentet fra ejendom og arbejdsdeling til lovgivning, regering og undertrykkelse.

after.title: Medfølelse og egenkærlighed
after.text: Rousseau skelner mellem ønsket om at bevare sig selv og den egenkærlighed, der afhænger af sammenligning med andre. Medfølelsen spiller en særskilt rolle.
after.angleObjective: Jeg vil forstå forskellen mellem amour de soi og amour-propre og undersøge medfølelsens betydning.

after.title: Hvem vinder ved fremskridtet?
after.text: Flere færdigheder og større rigdom kan følges af nye behov og større afhængighed. Rousseau spørger, hvad udviklingen betyder for frihed og lykke.
after.angleObjective: Jeg vil afprøve Rousseaus kritik af fremskridt uden på forhånd at sidestille alle forandringer med forfald.

before.name: Rousseau
before.description: En genfisk filosof, der skriver fra Paris, allerede berygtet for sin første afhandling, der hævdede, at kunsterne og videnskaberne havde fordærvet snarere end forbedret menneskeheden. Her går han videre: uligheden selv er ikke naturlig, men fremstillet af civilisationen. Hans tone er skiftevis analytisk og profetisk, og tilegnelsen til Genève — hans fødeby — indrammer argumentet som en personlig såvel som filosofisk handling.

before.name: Natural Man
before.description: Rousseaus rekonstruktion af, hvordan mennesker var, før samfundet: ensomme, sunde, selvtilstrækkelige, drevet af selvopholdelse og medlidenhed, men ikke af forfængelighed, sammenligning eller afhængighed af andre. Naturmennesket er ikke en ædel vild i romantisk forstand — det har næsten intet indre liv og intet sprog. Det er den målestok, hvormod Rousseau måler alt, hvad civilisationen har tilføjet, og alt, hvad den har ødelagt.

before.name: Amour-Propre
before.description: Det afgørende begreb, Rousseau skelner fra amour de soi (naturlig selvkærlighed). Amour-propre er ønsket om at blive agtet af andre — at blive værdsat, misundt, beundret. Det opstår kun i samfundet, når mennesker begynder at sammenligne sig, og det er ulighedens psykologiske motor. Når først folk bekymrer sig om, hvad andre mener om dem, vil de gøre hvad som helst for at fremstå overlegne. Ethvert socialt hierarki følger.

before.name: Private Property
before.description: Det øjeblik, hvor nogen indhegnede et stykke jord og kaldte det sit eget, er for Rousseau det borgerlige samfunds grundlæggende handling og oprindelsen til enhver form for politisk ulighed. Ejendom skaber skellet mellem rig og fattig; de rige skaber derefter regeringen for at beskytte, hvad de har; regeringen skaber loven; og loven gør uligheden permanent. Hele Afhandlingens anden halvdel sporer denne kæde.

before.name: The Academy of Dijon
before.description: Det lærde selskab, der stillede det prisspørgsmål, Rousseau besvarer: »Hvad er oprindelsen til ulighed blandt mennesker, og er den hjemlet af naturloven?« Rousseau vandt ikke prisen — hans svar var for langt, for radikalt og for fjendtligt over for de antagelser, der lå bag spørgsmålet. Han udgav det alligevel, og det blev en af de mest indflydelsesrige tekster i den politiske tænknings historie.

after.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
after.description: Han tilegner værket republikken Genève og undersøger ulighed gennem en hypotetisk fremstilling af menneskets udvikling. Han argumenterer både om menneskets følelser og om samfundets indretning.

after.name: Naturmennesket
after.description: Et tænkt menneske med få behov og få forbindelser til andre. Rousseau bruger det til at undersøge, hvilke egenskaber der kræver et udviklet samfund.

after.name: Egenkærligheden
after.description: En følelse, som afhænger af sammenligning og andres vurdering. Den adskiller sig fra den naturlige kærlighed til sig selv, der retter sig mod selvopholdelse.

after.name: Ejendommen
after.description: Ejendomsretten indgår i Rousseaus forklaring på forskellen mellem rig og fattig og på de regler og magtforhold, som siden befæster uligheden.

after.name: Akademiet i Dijon
after.description: Værket besvarer akademiets spørgsmål om ulighedens oprindelse, og om den er begrundet i naturloven. Rousseau skelner derfor mellem, hvordan uligheden opstår, og om den er retmæssig.

before.title: Opfindelsen af uligheden
before.body: Afhandlingen er det første vedholdende argument for, at ulighed ikke er naturlig, men konstrueret — at de forskelle i rigdom, magt og status, der præger ethvert kendt samfund, ikke er afspejlinger af naturlige forskelle mellem mennesker, men produkter af bestemte historiske udviklinger, frem for alt opfindelsen af privat ejendom. Denne idé er så grundigt optaget i moderne politisk tænkning, at det er svært at se, hvor radikal den var i 1755. Før Rousseau antog det meste af den politiske filosofi, at en eller anden form for hierarki var naturlig eller guddommeligt indstiftet. Efter Rousseau forskød bevisbyrden sig: enhver, der forsvarede ulighed, måtte forklare, hvordan den var opstået, og hvorfor den var berettiget. Marx, den socialistiske tradition, moderne egalitarisme og enhver kritik af strukturel ulighed i samfundsvidenskaberne nedstammer fra denne tekst.

before.title: Modoplysningen begynder
before.body: Voltaire læste Afhandlingen og skrev til Rousseau, at den gav ham lyst til at gå på alle fire. Spøgen tilslører uenighedens alvor. Oplysningstidens centrale forpligtelse var, at fornuft, videnskab og civilisation gør livet bedre. Rousseau hævdede det modsatte: at ethvert fremskridt i viden og samfundsorganisation er sket på bekostning af frihed, lighed og naturlig medfølelse. Dette modargument er aldrig forsvundet. Det dukker op igen i den romantiske filosofi, i Thoreaus Walden, i Frankfurterskolens kritik af den instrumentelle fornuft, hos enhver nutidig skribent, der har mistanke om, at teknologien gør os mere forbundne og mere ensomme på samme tid. Afhandlingen er den oprindelige tekst for den mistanke.

before.title: Medfølelse før fornuft
before.body: Rousseaus påstand om, at medlidenhed — en naturlig, før-rationel modvilje mod andres lidelse — er mere grundlæggende end fornuft, var en direkte udfordring til den filosofiske tradition fra Aristoteles gennem Hobbes. Hvis medfølelse kommer før tanken, så behøver moralen ikke at ræsonneres til eksistens; den behøver at blive beskyttet mod de rationaliseringer, der eroderer den. Denne idé påvirkede romantikken, formede den sentimentalistiske tradition i moralfilosofien og foregriber moderne forskning i moralpsykologi, der finder, at følelsesmæssige reaktioner går forud for og former moralske domme. Hvorvidt Rousseau har ret i følelsens forrang over fornuften, er stadig et åbent spørgsmål, men spørgsmålet selv — om moralen er bygget oppefra og ned eller ud fra hjertet — er et, han tvang ind i samtalens centrum.

after.title: Ulighed skal forklares
after.body: Rousseau undersøger, hvordan samfundets ordninger kan gøre forskelle varige og give dem rettens beskyttelse. Det inviterer læseren til at skelne mellem en forskels oprindelse og dens berettigelse.

after.title: Frihed og gensidig afhængighed
after.body: Samarbejde kan gøre mennesker dygtigere og samtidig mere afhængige. Værket undersøger, hvordan den afhængighed kan blive til herredømme, og hvorfor en regering, der skal beskytte friheden, kan ende med at ødelægge den.

after.title: At leve gennem andres blik
after.body: Den afsluttende del beskriver et menneske, der henter følelsen af sin egen værdi fra andres mening. Det gør forbindelsen mellem anseelse, konkurrence og personlig tilfredshed til et centralt spørgsmål i teksten.

Since this fortunate occasion partly makes up for what my efforts could not, I have allowed myself to consult here the zeal that moves me rather than the standing that should authorize me. Having had the good fortune to be born among you, how could I reflect on the equality nature established between human beings, and the inequality they themselves have introduced, without also reflecting on the deep wisdom by which both are combined in your state in the manner most in keeping with natural law, most favorable to society, to public order, and to individual happiness? In searching for the best rules common sense can lay down for the constitution of a government, I have been so struck to find them all already in force in yours that, even had I not been born within your walls, I would have felt it my duty to offer this portrait of human society to that people which, more than any other, seems to possess its greatest advantages and to have best guarded against its abuses.

onboardingChanges.before:
The Discourse on the Origin and Basis of Inequality Among Mankind asks a question that sounds simple and turns out to be explosive: where does inequality come from? Rousseau's answer is that natural inequality — differences in strength or intelligence — is trivial compared to the moral and political inequality that civilization creates. He constructs a speculative history of the human race from a solitary, self-sufficient natural state through the invention of property, agriculture, and government, arguing that each step made humans more dependent on each other and more unequal. The famous line — 'The first person who, having enclosed a plot of land, took it into his head to say this is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him, was the true founder of civil society' — captures the argument's force.

Written in 1754 as a response to a prize question from the Academy of Dijon and published in 1755, the Discourse is one of the founding texts of modern political philosophy. It broke with the Enlightenment optimism of Voltaire and the philosophes by arguing that civilization had not improved humanity but corrupted it — that the arts, sciences, and social institutions the Enlightenment celebrated were the very mechanisms of inequality and dependence. The argument influenced the French Revolution, Romantic philosophy, Marx's account of alienation, and every subsequent critique of progress that asks whether modernity has made people freer or more thoroughly controlled.
onboardingChanges.after:
Where do differences in wealth, power, and esteem come from? Rousseau distinguishes natural differences, such as age and strength, from moral or political inequality created through human conventions and institutions. He asks how property, the division of labor, and dependence enlarge those differences.

Published in 1755, the work here comprises a dedication to Geneva, a preface, and two main parts. The first examines a hypothetical human being before social life; the second follows developments toward property, government, and arbitrary power. Rousseau presents conjectural reasoning rather than a documented history of humanity.

before.title: The state of nature — thought experiment or history?
before.text: Rousseau describes a solitary, peaceful natural human who needs almost nothing and depends on no one. He insists this is not history but a tool for measuring how far civilization has taken us from our original condition. Watch where he treats it as hypothetical and where he seems to believe it.
before.angleObjective: I want to read the Discourse as a thought experiment about human nature — to understand what Rousseau thinks we were before society shaped us, and whether his 'natural man' is a real claim or a philosophical device.

before.title: Property as the origin of all evil.
before.text: Rousseau's most radical claim: the invention of private property is the moment everything goes wrong. Before property, inequality was trivial. After it, every form of domination follows. Track how he builds the case — and whether it convinces.
before.angleObjective: I want to follow Rousseau's argument that private property is the root of political inequality — to see exactly how he connects the act of enclosure to slavery, war, and the state.

before.title: Compassion before reason.
before.text: Rousseau argues that natural man has two basic drives: self-preservation and pity — a natural aversion to seeing others suffer. Reason comes later and actually weakens compassion. This reversal of the Enlightenment hierarchy is one of the most provocative claims in the text.
before.angleObjective: I want to trace Rousseau's claim that compassion is more fundamental than reason — that pity is natural while reflection is a corruption — and to test it against my own intuitions about what makes people moral.

before.title: Against progress.
before.text: The Enlightenment said civilization improves humanity. Rousseau said it enslaves us. The Discourse is the first systematic argument that progress is not what it seems — that every advance in knowledge, technology, and social organization has come at the cost of freedom and equality.
before.angleObjective: I want to read the Discourse as the founding critique of progress — Rousseau's case that civilization has made us more dependent, more unequal, and less free — and to decide how much of it still holds.

after.title: What is natural?
after.text: Rousseau separates what humans owe to nature from what life among others has made them. Follow the assumptions behind his original human being.
after.angleObjective: I want to examine what the state of nature explains and which assumptions that explanation needs.

after.title: Property and dependence
after.text: Land, divided labor, and shared rules change human relationships. Watch the intervening steps that connect possession to political power.
after.angleObjective: I want to follow the argument from property and labor to laws, government, and oppression.

after.title: Compassion and comparative self-love
after.text: Rousseau distinguishes self-preservation from the self-love that depends on comparison with others. Compassion plays a separate role.
after.angleObjective: I want to understand amour de soi and amour-propre and examine the role of compassion.

after.title: Who benefits from progress?
after.text: Greater skills and wealth can bring new needs and dependence. Rousseau asks what development means for freedom and happiness.
after.angleObjective: I want to test the critique of progress without assuming that every change must mean decline.

before.name: Rousseau
before.description: A Genevan philosopher writing from Paris, already notorious for his first Discourse arguing that the arts and sciences had corrupted rather than improved humanity. Here he goes further: inequality itself is not natural but manufactured by civilization. His tone is alternately analytical and prophetic, and the dedication to Geneva — his native city — frames the argument as a personal as well as philosophical act.

before.name: Natural Man
before.description: Rousseau's reconstruction of what humans were like before society: solitary, healthy, self-sufficient, moved by self-preservation and pity but not by vanity, comparison, or dependence on others. Natural man is not a noble savage in the romantic sense — he has almost no inner life and no language. He is the baseline against which Rousseau measures everything civilization has added and everything it has destroyed.

before.name: Amour-Propre
before.description: The crucial concept Rousseau distinguishes from amour de soi (natural self-love). Amour-propre is the desire to be esteemed by others — to be valued, envied, admired. It arises only in society, when humans begin to compare themselves, and it is the psychological engine of inequality. Once people care what others think of them, they will do anything to be seen as superior. Every social hierarchy follows.

before.name: Private Property
before.description: The moment someone enclosed a piece of land and called it his own is, for Rousseau, the founding act of civil society and the origin of every form of political inequality. Property creates the division between rich and poor; the rich then create government to protect what they have; government creates law; and law makes inequality permanent. The entire second half of the Discourse traces this chain.

before.name: The Academy of Dijon
before.description: The learned society that posed the prize question Rousseau is answering: 'What is the origin of inequality among men, and is it authorized by natural law?' Rousseau did not win the prize — his answer was too long, too radical, and too hostile to the assumptions behind the question. He published it anyway, and it became one of the most influential texts in the history of political thought.

after.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
after.description: He dedicates the work to the Republic of Geneva and examines inequality through a conjectural account of human development, connecting human feelings with social arrangements.

after.name: Natural man
after.description: A hypothetical human with few needs and few ties to others, used to examine which capacities require a developed society.

after.name: Amour-propre
after.description: A feeling dependent on comparison and the judgment of others, distinguished from the natural self-love directed toward self-preservation.

after.name: Property
after.description: Property rights help explain the division between rich and poor and the institutions that subsequently make inequality secure.

after.name: The Academy of Dijon
after.description: The work answers the academy’s question about the origin of inequality and whether natural law authorizes it. Rousseau therefore distinguishes its emergence from its justification.

before.title: The Invention of Inequality
before.body: The Discourse is the first sustained argument that inequality is not natural but constructed — that the differences in wealth, power, and status that define every known society are not reflections of natural differences between people but products of specific historical developments, above all the invention of private property. This idea is so thoroughly absorbed into modern political thought that it is difficult to see how radical it was in 1755. Before Rousseau, most political philosophy assumed that some form of hierarchy was natural or divinely ordained. After Rousseau, the burden of proof shifted: anyone defending inequality had to explain how it arose and why it was justified. Marx, the socialist tradition, modern egalitarianism, and every critique of structural inequality in the social sciences descend from this text.

before.title: The Counter-Enlightenment Begins
before.body: Voltaire read the Discourse and wrote to Rousseau that it made him want to walk on all fours. The joke masks the seriousness of the disagreement. The Enlightenment's central commitment was that reason, science, and civilization make life better. Rousseau argued the opposite: that every advance in knowledge and social organization has come at the cost of freedom, equality, and natural compassion. This counter-argument has never gone away. It reappears in Romantic philosophy, in Thoreau's Walden, in the Frankfurt School's critique of instrumental reason, in every contemporary writer who suspects that technology is making us more connected and more lonely at the same time. The Discourse is the original text of that suspicion.

before.title: Compassion Before Reason
before.body: Rousseau's claim that pity — a natural, pre-rational aversion to the suffering of others — is more fundamental than reason was a direct challenge to the philosophical tradition from Aristotle through Hobbes. If compassion comes before thought, then morality does not need to be reasoned into existence; it needs to be protected from the rationalizations that erode it. This idea influenced Romanticism, shaped the sentimentalist tradition in moral philosophy, and anticipates modern research in moral psychology that finds emotional responses preceding and shaping moral judgments. Whether Rousseau is right about the priority of feeling over reason is still an open question, but the question itself — whether morality is built from the head down or the heart out — is one he forced into the center of the conversation.

after.title: Explaining inequality
after.body: Rousseau examines how social arrangements make differences durable and give them legal protection. The reader is invited to distinguish a difference’s origin from its justification.

after.title: Freedom and dependence
after.body: Cooperation can develop human abilities while increasing dependence. The work asks how that dependence becomes domination and how a government intended to protect freedom can end up destroying it.

after.title: Living through others’ judgments
after.body: The conclusion portrays people whose sense of their own worth depends on others’ opinions. It makes esteem, competition, and personal satisfaction central questions for the reader.

authorNotesChanges.sourceFrench: ( Note  1 ) Hérodote raconte qu’après le meurtre du faux Smerdis, les sept libérateurs  de la Perse s’étant assemblés pour délibérer sur la forme de gouvernement  qu’ils donneraient à l’Etat, Otanès opina fortement pour la république; avis  d’autant plus extraordinaire dans la bouche d’un satrape qu’outre la prétention  qu’il pouvait avoir à l’empire, les Grands craignent plus que la mort une sorte  de gouvernement qui les force à respecter les hommes. Otanès, comme on peut  bien croire, ne fut pointé écouté et, voyant qu’on allait procéder à l’élection  d’un monarque, lui qui ne voulait ni obéir ni commander, céda volontairement  aux autres concurrents son droit à la couronne, demandant pour tout  dédommagement d’être libre et indépendant, lui et sa postérité, ce qui lui fut  accordé. Quand Hérodote ne nous apprendrait pas la restriction qui fut mise à  ce privilège, il faudrait nécessairement la supposer; autrement Otanès, ne  reconnaissant aucune sorte de loi et n’ayant de compte à rendre à personne,  aurait été tout-puissant dans l’Etat et plus puissant que le roi même. Mais il  n’y avait guère d’apparence qu’un homme capable de se contenter en pareil cas  d’un tel privilège fût capable d’en abuser. En effet, on ne voit pas que ce  droit ait jamais causé le moindre trouble dans le royaume, ni par le sage  Otanès, ni aucun de ses descendants.
after: Herodot fortæller, at Persiens syv befriere efter drabet på den falske Smerdis samledes for at drøfte, hvilken regeringsform de skulle give staten. Otanes talte stærkt for republikken. Det var et så meget mere usædvanligt synspunkt fra en satrap, som han selv kunne gøre krav på tronen, og stormænd frygter en regeringsform, der tvinger dem til at respektere andre mennesker, mere end døden. Som man kan tænke sig, blev Otanes ikke hørt. Da han så, at man ville vælge en monark, gav han, som hverken ville adlyde eller befale, frivilligt afkald på sin ret til kronen til fordel for de andre kandidater. Som eneste erstatning bad han om, at han selv og hans efterkommere måtte være frie og uafhængige, og det blev tilstået ham. Selv hvis Herodot ikke havde fortalt os, hvilken begrænsning der blev lagt på dette privilegium, måtte vi nødvendigvis forudsætte en sådan. Ellers ville Otanes, som hverken anerkendte nogen lov eller stod til ansvar over for nogen, have været almægtig i staten og mægtigere end kongen selv. Men det var næppe sandsynligt, at et menneske, der i en sådan situation kunne nøjes med et sådant privilegium, ville misbruge det. Man ser da heller ikke, at denne ret nogensinde skabte den mindste uro i riget, hverken gennem den kloge Otanes eller nogen af hans efterkommere.

authorNotesChanges.sourceFrench: ( Note  2 ) Dès mon premier pas je m'appuie avec confiance sur une de ces autorités  respectables pour les philosophes, parce qu'elles viennent d'une raison solide  et sublime qu'eux seuls savent trouver et sentir. "Quelque  intérêt que nous ayons à nous connaître nous-mêmes, je ne sais si nous ne connaissons  pas mieux tout ce qui n'est pas nous. Pourvus par la nature d'organes  uniquement destinés à notre conservation, nous ne les employons qu'à recevoir  les impressions étrangères, nous ne cherchons qu'à nous répandre au-dehors, et  à exister hors de nous; trop occupés à multiplier les fonctions de nos sens et  à augmenter l'étendue extérieure de notre être, rarement faisons-nous usage de  ce sens intérieur qui nous réduit à nos vraies dimensions et qui sépare de nous  tout ce qui n'en est pas. C'est cependant de ce sens dont il faut nous servir,  si nous voulons nous connaître; c'est le seul par lequel nous puissions nous  juger. Mais comment donner à ce sens son activité et toute son étendue? Comment  dégager notre âme, dans laquelle il réside, de toutes les illusions de notre  esprit? Nous avons perdu l'habitude de l'employer, elle est demeurée sans  exercice au milieu du tumulte de nos sensations corporelles, elle s'est  desséchée par le feu de nos passions; le coeur, l'esprit, le sens, tout a  travaillé contre elle." Hist.  Nat. T4, p. 151, De la Nat. de l'homme .
after: Allerede ved mit første skridt støtter jeg mig tillidsfuldt til en af de autoriteter, som filosoffer må respektere, fordi de udspringer af en solid og ophøjet fornuft, som kun de forstår at finde og værdsætte.

»Uanset hvor stor interesse vi har i at kende os selv, ved jeg ikke, om vi ikke kender alt andet bedre. Naturen har udstyret os med organer, der udelukkende er bestemt til vores selvopholdelse, men vi bruger dem kun til at modtage indtryk udefra. Vi søger kun at brede os udad og eksistere uden for os selv. Vi er så optaget af at mangedoble sansernes funktioner og udvide vores væsens ydre rækkevidde, at vi sjældent bruger den indre sans, som fører os tilbage til vores virkelige mål og skiller alt det fra os, som ikke er os selv. Alligevel er det denne sans, vi må bruge, hvis vi vil kende os selv; kun gennem den kan vi bedømme os selv. Men hvordan giver vi denne sans dens aktivitet og fulde rækkevidde? Hvordan befrier vi vores sjæl, hvor den findes, fra alle forstandens illusioner? Vi har mistet vanen med at bruge den. Den er forblevet uøvet midt i de kropslige sansningers larm og er tørret ud af lidenskabernes ild. Hjertet, forstanden, sanserne — alt har modarbejdet den.« _Naturhistorie_, bind 4, s. 151, »Om menneskets natur«.

authorNotesChanges.sourceFrench: ( Note  3 ) Les changements qu'un long usage de marcher sur deux pieds a pu produire  dans la conformation de l'homme, les rapports qu'on observe encore entre ses  bras et les jambes antérieures des quadrupèdes et l'induction tirée de leur  manière de marcher ont pu faire naître des doutes sur celle qui devait nous  être la plus naturelle. Tous les enfants commencent par marcher à quatre pieds  et ont besoin de notre exemple et de nos leçons pour apprendre à se tenir  debout. Il y a même des nations sauvages, telles que les Hottentots qui,  négligeant beaucoup les enfants, les laissent marcher sur les mains si  longtemps qu'ils ont ensuite bien de la peine à les redresser; autant en font  les enfants des Caraïbes des Antilles. Il y a divers exemples d'hommes  quadrupèdes et je pourrais entre autres citer celui de cet enfant qui fut  trouvé, en 1344, auprès de Hesse où il avait été nourri par des loups et qui  disait depuis à la cour du prince Henri que, s'il n'eût tenu qu'à lui, il eût  mieux aimé retourner avec eux que de vivre parmi les hommes. Il avait tellement  pris l'habitude de marcher comme ces animaux qu'il fallut lui attacher des  pièces de bois qui le forçaient à se tenir debout et en équilibre sur ses deux  pieds. Il en était de même de l'enfant qu'on trouva en 1694 dans les forêts de  Lituanie et qui vivait parmi les ours. Il ne donnait, dit M. de Condillac,  aucune marque de raison, marchait sur ses pieds et sur ses mains, n'avait aucun  langage et formait des sons qui ne ressemblaient en rien à ceux d'un homme. Le  petit sauvage d'Hanovre qu'on mena il y a plusieurs années à la cour  d'Angleterre, avait toutes les peines du monde à s'assujettir à marcher sur  deux pieds et l'on trouva en 1719 deux autres sauvages dans les Pyrénées, qui  couraient par les montagnes à la manière des quadrupèdes. Quant à ce qu'on  pourrait objecter que c'est se priver de l'usage des mains dont nous tirons  tant d'avantages, outre que l'exemple des singes montre que la main peut fort  bien être employée des deux manières, cela prouverait seulement que l'homme  peut donner à ses membres une destination plus commode que celle de la nature,  et non que la nature a destiné l'homme à marcher autrement qu'elle ne lui  enseigne. Mais il y a, ce me semble, de beaucoup  meilleures raisons, à dire pour soutenir que l'homme est un bipède.  Premièrement quand on ferait voir qu'il a pu d'abord être conformé autrement  que nous le voyons et cependant devenir enfin ce qu'il est, ce n'en serait pas  assez pour conclure que cela se soit fait ainsi. Car, après avoir montré la  possibilité de ces changements, il faudrait encore, avant que de les admettre,  en montrer au moins la vraisemblance. De plus, si les bras de l'homme  paraissent avoir pu lui servir de jambes au besoin, c'est la seule observation  favorable à ce système, sur un grand nombre d'autres qui lui sont contraires.  Les principales sont: que la manière dont la tête de l'homme est attachée à son  corps, au lieu de diriger sa vue horizontalement, comme l'ont tous les autres  animaux, et comme il l'a lui-même en marchant debout, lui eût tenu, marchant à  quatre pieds, les yeux directement fichés vers la terre, situation très peu  favorable à la conservation de l'individu; que la queue qui lui manque, et dont  il n'a que faire marchant à deux pieds, est utile aux quadrupèdes, et qu'aucun  d'eux n'en est privé; que le sein de la femme, très bien situé pour un bipède  qui tient son enfant dans ses bras, l'est si mal pour un quadrupède que nul ne  l'a placé de cette manière; que le train de derrière étant d'une excessive  hauteur à proportion des jambes de devant, ce qui fait que marchant à quatre  nous nous traînons sur les genoux, le tout eût fait un animal mal proportionné  et marchant peu commodément; que s'il eût posé le pied à plat ainsi que la  main, il aurait eu dans la jambe postérieure une articulation de moins que les  autres animaux, savoir celle qui joint le canon au tibia, et qu'en ne posant  que la pointe du pied, comme il aurait sans doute été contraint de faire, le tarse,  sans parler de la pluralité des os qui le composent, paraît trop gros pour  tenir lieu de canon et ses articulations avec le métatarse et le tibia trop  rapprochées pour donner à la jambe humaine dans cette situation la même  flexibilité qu'ont celles des quadrupèdes. L'exemple des enfants étant pris  dans un âge où les forces naturelles ne sont point encore développées ni les  membres raffermis, ne conclut rien du tout et j'aimerais autant dire que les  chiens ne sont pas destinés à marcher, parce qu'ils ne font que ramper quelques  semaines après leur naissance. Les faits particuliers ont encore peu de force  contre la pratique universelle de tous les hommes, même des nations qui,  n'ayant eu aucune communication avec les autres, n'avaient pu rien imiter d'elles.  Un enfant abandonné dans une forêt avant que de pouvoir marcher, et nourri par  quelque bête, aura suivi l'exemple de sa nourrice en s'exerçant à marcher comme  elle; l'habitude lui aura pu donner des facilités qu'il ne tenait point de la  nature; et comme des manchots parviennent à force d'exercice à faire avec leurs  pieds tout ce que nous faisons de nos mains, il sera parvenu enfin à employer  ses mains à l'usage des pieds.
after: De forandringer, som lang tids gang på to ben kan have frembragt i menneskets kropsbygning, de ligheder, man stadig ser mellem dets arme og de firbenede dyrs forben, og slutninger ud fra deres gang kan have vakt tvivl om, hvilken måde at gå på der er mest naturlig for os. Alle børn begynder med at gå på alle fire og behøver vores eksempel og undervisning for at lære at stå oprejst. Der findes endda vilde folkeslag, som hottentotterne, der forsømmer børnene så meget, at de lader dem gå på hænderne så længe, at de senere har svært ved at få dem til at rette sig op. Det samme gælder karibernes børn på Antillerne. Der findes flere eksempler på mennesker, som gik på alle fire. Blandt dem kunne jeg nævne barnet, som i 1344 blev fundet ved Hessen, hvor ulve havde opfostret det. Senere sagde det ved fyrst Henriks hof, at hvis det selv havde kunnet vælge, ville det hellere være vendt tilbage til ulvene end leve blandt mennesker. Det var så vant til at gå som disse dyr, at man måtte spænde træstykker på det for at tvinge det til at stå oprejst og holde balancen på to fødder. Det samme gjaldt barnet, som i 1694 blev fundet i Litauens skove og havde levet blandt bjørne. Det viste, siger hr. de Condillac, ingen tegn på fornuft, gik på fødder og hænder, havde intet sprog og frembragte lyde, som slet ikke lignede et menneskes. Den lille vilde fra Hannover, som for nogle år siden blev ført til det engelske hof, havde uhyre svært ved at vænne sig til at gå på to ben. I 1719 fandt man desuden to andre vilde i Pyrenæerne, som løb gennem bjergene på alle fire.

Man kunne indvende, at mennesket derved ville miste brugen af hænderne, som giver os så mange fordele. Men abernes eksempel viser, at hånden godt kan bruges på begge måder. Indvendingen ville kun bevise, at mennesket kan give sine lemmer en mere bekvem anvendelse end den naturlige, ikke at naturen har bestemt det til at gå anderledes, end hun lærer det.

Der findes imidlertid efter min mening langt bedre grunde til at hævde, at mennesket er tobenet. For det første ville det ikke være nok til at slutte, at forløbet faktisk havde været sådan, selv om man kunne vise, at det oprindeligt kunne have haft en anden kropsbygning og alligevel være blevet, som vi ser det nu. Efter at have vist forandringernes mulighed måtte man i det mindste også vise deres sandsynlighed, før man antog dem. Desuden er det, at menneskets arme om nødvendigt kunne have tjent som ben, den eneste iagttagelse, der støtter denne forklaring, mens en lang række taler imod den.

De vigtigste modargumenter er følgende. Hovedets placering på kroppen ville ved gang på alle fire rette øjnene lige ned mod jorden, i stedet for at rette blikket vandret, som hos alle andre dyr og hos mennesket selv, når det går oprejst. Det er en meget ugunstig stilling for individets bevarelse. Halen, som mennesket mangler og ikke behøver ved gang på to ben, er nyttig for firbenede dyr, og ingen af dem mangler den. Kvindens bryst er meget velplaceret for et tobenet væsen, som holder sit barn i armene, men så dårligt placeret for et firbenet, at ingen af dem har det sådan. Bagkroppen er alt for høj i forhold til forbenene, så vi må slæbe os frem på knæene, når vi går på alle fire. Det hele ville derfor udgøre et dårligt proportioneret dyr med en ubekvem gang. Hvis mennesket satte hele foden i jorden ligesom hånden, ville det have ét led mindre i bagbenet end andre dyr, nemlig leddet mellem mellemfoden og skinnebenet. Hvis det kun støttede på tæerne, som det uden tvivl ville være nødt til, synes fodroden at være for stor til at gøre det ud for den lange mellemfodsknogle, selv uden at medregne de mange knogler, den består af. Dens led med mellemfoden og skinnebenet ligger også for tæt til i denne stilling at give menneskebenet samme smidighed som de firbenede dyrs.

Eksemplet med børn beviser intet, fordi det gælder en alder, hvor de naturlige kræfter endnu ikke er udviklet, og lemmerne ikke er blevet faste. Jeg kunne lige så godt sige, at hunde ikke er bestemt til at gå, fordi de kun kryber i ugerne efter fødslen. Enkelttilfælde vejer heller ikke tungt imod den almindelige praksis hos alle mennesker, selv hos folk, der aldrig har haft forbindelse med andre og derfor ikke har kunnet efterligne dem. Et barn, der efterlades i en skov, før det kan gå, og opfostres af et dyr, vil følge sin ammes eksempel og øve sig i at gå som hende. Vanen kan have givet det færdigheder, det ikke havde fra naturen. Ligesom mennesker uden arme gennem øvelse lærer at gøre alt det med fødderne, som vi gør med hænderne, kan barnet til sidst have lært at bruge hænderne som fødder.

authorNotesChanges.sourceFrench: ( Note  4 ) S'il se trouvait parmi mes lecteurs quelque assez mauvais physicien pour me  faire des difficultés sur la supposition de cette fertilité naturelle de la  terre, je vais lui répondre par le passage suivant: "Comme  les végétaux tirent pour leur nourriture beaucoup plus de substance de l'air et  de l'eau qu'ils n'en tirent de la terre, il arrive qu'en pourrissant ils  rendent à la terre plus qu'ils n'en ont tiré; d'ailleurs une forêt détermine  les eaux de la pluie en arrêtant les vapeurs. Ainsi dans un bois que l'on  conserverait bien longtemps sans y toucher, la couche de terre qui sert à la  végétation augmenterait considérablement; mais les animaux rendant moins à la  terre qu'ils n'en tirent, et les hommes faisant des consommations énormes de  bois et de plantes pour le feu et pour d'autres usages, il s'ensuit que la  couche de terre végétale d'un pays habité doit toujours diminuer et devenir  enfin comme le terrain de l'Arabie Pétrée, et comme celui de tant d'autres  provinces de l'Orient, qui est en effet le climat le plus anciennement habité,  où l'on ne trouve que du sel et des sables, car le sel fixe des plantes et des  animaux reste, tandis que toutes les autres parties se volatilisent." M.  de Buffon, Hist. Nat . On  peut ajouter à cela la preuve de fait par la quantité d'arbres et de plantes de  toute espèce, dont étaient remplies presque toutes les îles désertes qui ont  été découvertes dans ces derniers siècles, et par ce que l'Histoire nous  apprend des forêts immenses qu'il a fallu abattre par toute la terre à mesure  qu'elle s'est peuplée et policée. Sur quoi je ferai encore les trois remarques  suivantes. L'une que s'il y a une sorte de végétaux qui puissent compenser la  déperdition de matière végétale qui se fait par les animaux, selon le  raisonnement de M. de Buffon, ce sont surtout les bois, dont les têtes et les  feuilles rassemblent et s'approprient plus d'eaux et de vapeurs que ne font les  autres plantes. La seconde, que la destruction du sol, c'est-à-dire la perte de  la substance propre à la végétation doit s'accélérer à proportion que la terre  est plus cultivée et que les habitants plus industrieux consomment en plus  grande abondance ses productions de toute espèce. Ma troisième et plus  importante remarque est que les fruits des arbres fournissent à l'animal une  nourriture plus abondante que ne peuvent faire les autres végétaux, expérience  que j'ai faite moi-même, en comparant les produits de deux terrains égaux en  grandeur et en qualité, l'un couvert de châtaigniers et l'autre semé de blé.
after: Hvis nogen af mine læsere er så dårlig en naturforsker, at han vil gøre indvendinger mod antagelsen om jordens naturlige frugtbarhed, vil jeg svare ham med følgende passage:

»Da planterne til deres næring henter langt mere stof fra luften og vandet end fra jorden, giver de ved forrådnelsen mere tilbage til jorden, end de har taget fra den. Desuden fremkalder en skov regn ved at standse vanddampene. I en skov, der blev bevaret urørt meget længe, ville det jordlag, som nærer væksten, derfor blive betydeligt tykkere. Men dyrene giver mindre tilbage til jorden, end de tager fra den, og menneskene bruger enorme mængder træ og planter til brændsel og andre formål. Derfor må muldlaget i et beboet land stadig blive tyndere og til sidst ligne jorden i Arabia Petraea og så mange andre egne af Østen, som jo er de længst beboede områder. Dér finder man kun salt og sand, for planternes og dyrenes ikke-flygtige salte bliver tilbage, mens alle de andre bestanddele fordamper.« Hr. de Buffon, Naturhistorie.

Hertil kan man føje den faktiske støtte i mængden af træer og planter af alle slags, som fyldte næsten alle de ubeboede øer, der er blevet opdaget i de seneste århundreder, og i historiens beretninger om de vældige skove, man har måttet fælde over hele jorden, efterhånden som den blev befolket og civiliseret. Jeg vil her gøre tre yderligere bemærkninger. For det første: Hvis nogen planter kan opveje det tab af plantestof, dyrene ifølge hr. de Buffons ræsonnement forårsager, er det især træerne. Deres kroner og blade opsamler og optager mere vand og damp end andre planter. For det andet må jordens ødelæggelse, det vil sige tabet af det stof, som planterne lever af, gå hurtigere, jo mere jorden dyrkes, og jo større mængder af alle dens frembringelser de mere foretagsomme indbyggere bruger. Min tredje og vigtigste bemærkning er, at træernes frugter giver dyrene rigeligere føde end andre planter kan. Det har jeg selv undersøgt ved at sammenligne udbyttet fra to stykker jord af samme størrelse og kvalitet, det ene bevokset med kastanjetræer og det andet tilsået med korn.
